FDWWVXAH.title: Michigan’s newest newsrooms are AI machines built on others’ reporting
FDWWVXAH.markdown:
### Earlier this spring, a new local newsroom appeared in Grand Traverse County seemingly overnight. The site, called Prism News, publishes two to six local stories a day under the bylines of nearly 40 journalists.

### But here’s the catch: None of those reporters are human.

Editor's note

About a month after we initially published this story, Prism took down its 200 sites, including the local news site focused on Grand Traverse County.Learn more.

Instead of traditional reporters, the site copies and rewrites the work of other outlets through artificial intelligence.

In fact, the Grand Traverse Prism news site is just one of more than 200 AI-generated publications run by Prism across the United States. Prism has one other news site in Michigan, in Iron County.

Those sites can be split into two categories: publications focused on hobby communities (like sourdough baking or bonsai gardening) and local news coverage.

[ Prism announced its launch in press materials in May 2026](https://www.newsfilecorp.com/release/298739/Prism-Media-Launches-Prism-News-an-AINative-Publishing-Platform-Operating-More-Than-200-Niche-Publications-Nationwide), saying “the launch arrives at a difficult moment for American media. There are now 213 counties with no local news source at all, and another 1,524 down to a single outlet. Roughly 50 million Americans live in what researchers call a news desert.”

In that news release, Prism said it was built to address that gap in coverage. How Prism plans to do that — with no original coverage of its own — is unknown.

IPR was in contact with Prism co-founder Daniel Koren and requested an interview multiple times. After repeated requests were turned down, IPR sent a list of questions to Koren. Koren did not respond in time for this story.

**Local stories without local reporting**

At first glance, Prism’s stories look authentic.

They feature real people, real places and real events from northern Michigan. But unlike a traditional newsroom, Prism's reporting process is almost entirely powered by artificial intelligence.

[ One person featured in a Prism article is Jonah Ezell](https://www.prismnews.com/local/grand-traverse-mi/teen-farmer-grows-pasture-raised-chicken-business-in-grand), a young chicken farmer in northern Michigan.

“I never talked to anybody at all from Prism,” said Ezell. “I guess they just did their own thing. I got no contact at all with them."

Instead, Prism summarized an [ existing story produced by UpNorthLive](https://upnorthlive.com/news/local/grand-traverse-county-teen-runs-good-father-farms-selling-pasture-raised-non-gmo-chickens-grand-traverse-county) and used real photos of Ezell's farm and details from UpNorthLive’s original reporting.

According to LinkedIn, [ the Israel-based startup behind Prism has just four employees](https://www.linkedin.com/company/prismedia-ai/people/). Its model, as stated in the launch material, is to create hundreds of local news and hobby sites, automate production and generate advertising revenue at scale.

“It's really just a summary of a story,” Ezell said as he read over Prism’s coverage of his story. “There's nothing else to it.”

Though Prism’s AI largely summarizes reporting already produced by other news organizations, factual errors and discrepancies do appear.

One article incorrectly placed Traverse City in southwest Michigan. Another misstated how much Michigan spends sending children out of state for mental health care. Another stated the wrong reason for why a recall petition was set in motion against Grand Traverse County’s prosecuting attorney.

In [ Prism’s AI Disclosure](https://www.prismnews.com/disclaimer), the company explains that “individual articles are not hand-edited before publication (but that) the publication as a whole is supervised by people”. While Prism writes that automated quality and moderation checks are run before publishing, they do acknowledge that “the system can still make mistakes: names can be misspelled, dates can be misordered, and context can be missed.”

How Prism runs human moderation and fact-checking is unclear.

Whether those standards apply to the “AI-illustrated” photos which accompany Prism’s articles is also unclear, in that many photos depict people and places incorrectly.

Those AI-generated photos often accompany real photos taken from other outlets. The captions of photos are the one place real outlets are credited, although that does not always happen.

**AI-generated images raise additional concerns**

The AI-generated image that accompanied Ezell's story appeared realistic at first glance, but included details that weren't accurate.

The illustration showed Ezell sitting on a hill overlooking his chickens at sunset.

When shown the image, Ezell said it looked close — but not quite right.

“It almost passes,” he said. “The problem is, I don't have any structures like that ... That's just not me. It's not my farm."

Ezell’s photo is less egregious than others. In other AI-generated images, people are depicted as being a __different__[ race](https://www.prismnews.com/local/grand-traverse-mi/three-grand-traverse-county-residents-honored-for-stopping). 

[on local flooding showed a group of people in a life raft being rescued by sheriff deputies. That did not happen.](https://www.prismnews.com/local/grand-traverse-mi/grand-traverse-county-declares-emergency-as-boardman-river)

__Another story__Ezell’s AI photo had smaller inaccuracies, but even those can leave readers with the wrong impression.

“If people look at that chicken tractor, and it's a little bit off, like it's really big … people could think that I'm like this really huge guy that I'm really not,” he said. “If you got one or two details more wrong, you could have a completely different opinion on me.”

**‘Pink slime’**

MediaWise director and Poynter Institute faculty member Alex Mahadevan said Prism is part of a growing network of so-called "pink slime" news sites.

“Pink slime news sites are absolutely not new,” Mahadevan said. “They've been around since before 2016 … but now it is just so easy to set up a pink slime news site, which is a site that's run purely for cheap advertising dollars or to spread political misinformation."

Prism does not appear to spread political information, but that has been common with other pink slime networks. One of the largest, [ Metric Media, created an estimated 1,200 supposedly local news sites](https://www.wgbh.org/news/commentary/2021-11-03/follow-the-money-right-wing-funding-of-pink-slime-websites-tracked-in-new-study) and used them to 

[,](https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/516504-catholic-group-launches-97m-campaign-against-biden-targeting-swing-state)

__attack opponents__

__promote particular right wing political candidates and advance the interests of advocacy groups and corporate clients.__Earlier generations of pink slime sites often relied on algorithms or low-cost labor to scrape and rewrite stories from legitimate news outlets.

Now, artificial intelligence can greatly accelerate that process.

“There's just this fire hose of news stories that they can pump out and then basically post across social media,” Mahadevan said. “When people see it on social media, they just see an image ahead of a line in a deck. They don't know if it's from a credible news site so they're going to click it."

[ As of 2024, pink slime sites officially outnumbered real local news organizations.](https://www.newsguardtech.com/press/sad-milestone-fake-local-news-sites-now-outnumber-real-local-newspaper-sites-in-u-s/) Mahadevan said the growth of those sites creates two major problems.

The first is economic.

“It's crowding out legitimate local news,” Mahadevan said. “(Newsrooms) make money and get paid by doing the work. That is going to community meetings, that is going to county commission meetings, that's calling sources, that's spending the time to write up investigations. Sites like this essentially come in, they siphon away clicks, they siphon away ad dollars."

The second reason, he said, is that low-quality, AI-generated stories risk undermining trust in local journalism, historically one of the country's most trusted sources of news.

But maybe the larger issue is accountability.

“Journalism is an extremely human craft,” Mahadevan said. “Think about the number of ethical decisions you make throughout the reporting process, throughout the writing process, throughout the editing process. You are accountable to the people you cover. The machines that are pumping out and scraping your work are accountable to no one.”

IPR has since contacted Prism with corrections to several local stories.

Those corrections have since been made.

*This reporting is made possible by the Northern Michigan Journalism Collaborative, led by Bridge Michigan and Interlochen Public Radio, and funded by Press Forward Northern Michigan.*

22GNGKTK.title: Prism News shuts down network of more than 200 AI-generated local news sites
22GNGKTK.markdown:
### After only a few months of operation, Prism News’s network of more than 200 AI-generated publications – posing as local newsrooms and hobby sites – has closed.

This includes the local “AI-powered newsroom” *Prism Grand Traverse County, *which produced news articles about northwest Michigan. [As IPR reported in July](https://www.interlochenpublicradio.org/ipr-news/2026-07-16/michigans-newest-newsrooms-are-ai-machines-built-on-others-reporting), that coverage was created using artificial intelligence to aggregate news from local outlets and repurpose Prism’s slightly-altered articles under new bylines.

*Spin Class*, who also investigated Prism.

None of those bylines belonged to real people. Instead, they represented “AI-personas.” One of those personas even carried the title “Dr.” — Elena Rodriguez.

When Prism announced its launch in May, the Israel-based start up poised itself as an answer to news deserts across the United States. Despite that, Prism produced no original news coverage of its own.

Now, where Prism used to have hundreds of sites and thousands of articles, their website is empty with a line of text that reads, “We have currently completed our initial experiment. A big thank you to all who participated and gave their feedback. All activity is suspended for the foreseeable future.”

Facebook pages for Prism newsrooms across the country — including sites for Grand Traverse and Iron County — have been cleared of months of links to their news articles and short form content.

IPR has reached out to Prism for comment but has not received any response at the time of publishing.

4DRZXZ6U.title: ChatGPT is making up fake Guardian articles. Here’s how we’re responding
4DRZXZ6U.markdown:
Last month one of our journalists received an interesting email. A researcher had come across mention of a Guardian article, written by the journalist on a specific subject from a few years before. But the piece was proving elusive on our website and in search. Had the headline perhaps been changed since it was launched? Had it been removed intentionally from the website because of a problem we’d identified? Or had we been forced to take it down by the subject of the piece through legal means?

The reporter couldn’t remember writing the specific piece, but the headline certainly sounded like something they would have written. It was a subject they were identified with and had a record of covering. Worried that there may have been some mistake at our end, they asked colleagues to go back through our systems to track it down. Despite the detailed records we keep of all our content, and especially around deletions or legal issues, they could find no trace of its existence.

Why? Because it had never been written.

Luckily the researcher had told us that they had carried out their research using [ChatGPT](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/chatgpt). In response to being asked about articles on this subject, the AI had simply made some up. Its fluency, and the vast training data it is built on, meant that the existence of the invented piece even seemed believable to the person who absolutely hadn’t written it.

Huge amounts have been written about generative AI’s tendency to manufacture facts and events. But this specific wrinkle – the invention of sources – is particularly troubling for trusted news organisations and journalists whose inclusion adds legitimacy and weight to a persuasively written fantasy. And for readers and the wider information ecosystem, it opens up whole new questions about whether citations can be trusted in any way, and could well feed conspiracy theories about the mysterious removal of articles on sensitive issues that never existed in the first place.

If this seems like an edge case, it’s important to note that ChatGPT, from a cold start in November, [registered 100 million monthly users in January](https://www.reuters.com/technology/chatgpt-sets-record-fastest-growing-user-base-analyst-note-2023-02-01/). TikTok, unquestionably a digital phenomenon, took nine months to hit the same level. Since that point we’ve seen Microsoft implement the same technology in Bing, putting pressure on Google to follow suit with Bard.

They are now implementing these systems into Google Workspace and Microsoft 365, which have a [90% plus share of the market](https://www.statista.com/statistics/983299/worldwide-market-share-of-office-productivity-software/) between them. [A recent study](https://study.com/resources/perceptions-of-chatgpt-in-schools) of 1,000 students in the US found that 89% have used ChatGPT to help with a homework assignment. The technology, with all its faults, has been normalised at incredible speed, and is now at the heart of systems that act as the key point of discovery and creativity for a significant portion of the world.

Two days ago our archives team was contacted by a student asking about another missing article from a named journalist. There was again no trace of the article in our systems. The source? ChatGPT.

It’s easy to get sucked into the detail on generative AI, because it is inherently opaque. The ideas and implications, already explored by academics across multiple disciplines, are hugely complex, the technology is developing rapidly, and companies with huge existing market shares are integrating it as fast as they can to gain competitive advantages, disrupt each other and above all satisfy shareholders.

But the question for responsible news organisations is simple, and urgent: what can this technology do right now, and how can it benefit responsible reporting at a time when the wider information ecosystem is already under pressure from misinformation, polarisation and bad actors.

This is the question we are currently grappling with at the Guardian. And it’s why we haven’t yet announced a new format or product built on generative AI. Instead, we’ve created a working group and small engineering team to focus on learning about the technology, considering the public policy and IP questions around it, listening to academics and practitioners, talking to other organisations, consulting and training our staff, and exploring safely and responsibly how the technology performs when applied to journalistic use.

In doing this we have found that, along with asking how we can use generative AI, we are reflecting more and more on what journalism is for, and what makes it valuable. We are excited by the potential, but our first task must be to understand it, evaluate it and decode its potential impact on the wider world.

In the next few weeks we’ll be publishing a clear and concise explanation of how we plan to employ generative AI. In the simplest terms, we will continue to hold ourselves to the highest journalistic standards and remain accountable to our readers and the world for the journalism we publish. While so much has changed in the last six months, in this crucial respect, nothing has changed at all.

BKUHYT6T.title: Times journalists urged to make 'basic' checks after two 'humiliating' hoaxes
BKUHYT6T.markdown:
A newsroom boss at [The Times](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/the-times/) has described two fake interviews recently run by the newsbrand as “humiliating” and said “absolutely basic” questions were not asked.

Times associate editor Ian Brunskill told staff: “Twice in the past few weeks we’ve been caught out by fake interviews. One involved a bogus Al-generated case study provided by a dubious PR outfit, the other a fake email purporting to come from a high-profile figure in US politics…

“We should have been on our guard. We should have tried much harder to speak to the people concerned. If that’s not possible, why not?”

One of the incidents was revealed in September by Press Gazette: [The Times was among major UK and US newsbrands to publish interviews with ‘Anne Simmons’](https://pressgazette.co.uk/news/royal-cleaner-stories-removed-by-times-and-sun-after-authenticity-questions/), a purported royal cleaner who claimed to have worked for the Royal Family for more than a decade.

However there appears to be no record of someone called Anne Simmons having worked for Buckingham Palace or been vetted by security.

The articles, which largely shared cleaning tips from Simmons, appear to have been based on press releases sent out on behalf of a number of companies that claimed to have interviewed Simmons including: Edit Suits, Plumbworld, Playcasino, Plates Express and Pure Window Cleaning.

The Times appeared to have run with the story first in March, [with a piece headlined](https://archive.ph/PwKoW#selection-1721.42-1721.56): “How do you spruce up Buckingham Palace? A royal cleaner spills.”

The news website, and sister News UK brand The Sun, removed articles about Simmons after Press Gazette questioned their authenticity. Other publishers to have published “interviews” with Simmons included the [Daily Mail](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/home/you/article-14523871/A-royal-housekeeper-reveals-three-supermarket-essentials-used-spring-clean-Buckingham-Palace-bathrooms-one-just-35p.html), [Daily Express](https://www.express.co.uk/life-style/property/2057090/cleaner-Buckingham-Palace-hoover-alternative-slime), [New York Post](https://nypost.com/2025/05/14/entertainment/king-charles-has-banned-two-household-items-from-buckingham-palace/) and [Daily Mirror](https://www.mirror.co.uk/lifestyle/food-drink/royal-cleaning-expert-shares-10-35293603).

Press Gazette editor-in-chief Dominic Ponsford has called on the Independent Press Standards Organisation, which regulates all of the UK publishers above, [to investigate the “systematic failings](https://pressgazette.substack.com/p/express-had-most-ipso-breaches-in) which lead publishers to keep running fake, likely AI-generated, PR content”.

[Press Gazette has in the past few months uncovered around 100 examples of articles published by IPSO member publishers containing fictitious information supplied by dubious PR companies](https://pressgazette.co.uk/news/agencies-linked-to-missing-lottery-winners-bombard-journalists-with-fake-case-studies-ai/) that went unverified before being published.

Ponsford said: “IPSO-regulated publishers should be the last publications to be fooled by this stuff but they appear to be among the first.”

## Wrong Bill de Blasio: ‘They accepted my quote without vetting’

Then, last week, The Times published a supposed interview with former New York mayor Bill de Blasio about the policies of Zohran Mamdani, the frontrunner in the city’s current mayoral race.

De Blasio denied having given the interview and a Times spokesperson said its journalist “had been misled by an individual falsely claiming to be the former New York mayor”. The article was removed.

However Semafor revealed the journalist had emailed the wrong De Blasio and had inadvertently contacted a Long Island wine importer by the same name (but spelled as DeBlasio without a space).

[That De Blasio told Semafor](https://www.semafor.com/article/10/29/2025/british-newspaper-spoke-to-the-wrong-deblasio-not-an-imposter): “I never once said I was the mayor. He never addressed me as the mayor. So I just gave him my opinion.”

He also dispute the statement put out by The Times, telling [the Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/zohran-mamdani-andrew-cuomo-bill-de-blasio-8da7fc3331340c897d6a71f83e59ddc5): “In no way shape or form did I call myself the mayor. The reporter addressed me as Mr. DeBlasio and I answered him as Mr. DeBlasio. They accepted my quote without any vetting – now they’re blaming me?”

## Times memo: ‘Serious damage to our reputation’

In a memo sent to staff at the end of last week, [first reported by Deadline](https://deadline.com/2025/10/bill-de-blasio-fake-interview-humiliating-times-editor-says-1236603178/), Times associate editor Ian Brunskill urged the newsroom to ask more questions when speaking to sources.

He wrote: “The first hoax (which others fell for too) prompted not just ridicule but calls for the press regulator to launch a full investigation into standards. The second (our own “exclusive”, alas) led to a widely reported retraction and apology.

“Both humiliating episodes did serious damage to our reputation. Both could have been avoided by good practice and due diligence.

“There were red flags. An unknown PR company with no telephone number offering to put us in touch with an unknown ‘expert’ who could be interviewed only via email was one. A well-known public figure expressing a view completely at odds with his previous statements, and doing it from a personal Gmail address, was another.”

Listing questions that ought to have been asked, Brunskill continued: “We – reporters and editors – should be asking: Who is telling me this and why? How do I know they’re who they say they are? How plausible is what I’m being told? What can I do to check?

“Those questions are absolutely basic. Asking them should be second nature to anyone working for a paper with a long history of trusted reporting. There are no excuses.

“As a condition of employment, we’re bound by the Editors’ Code. It requires us to take care to avoid inaccuracy. If there’s a complaint, IPSO will expect us to show precisely what taking care involved. We can’t afford to be fooled.”

A spokesperson for IPSO said last week: “Press Gazette’s valuable reporting on the emerging phenomenon of AI-generated press releases is a useful reminder to editors and journalists of risks posed by large language models.

“Those regulated by IPSO are accountable for their content and must take care to satisfy themselves that their sources are accurate.

“The standards they have agreed to meet set them apart from non-regulated titles and help to maintain trust and credibility with readers.”

Email ** pged@pressgazette.co.uk** to point out mistakes, provide story tips or send in a letter for publication on our "Letters Page" blog

BNP9FRUN.title: Generative AI used to copy and clone French news media in French-speaking Africa | RSF
BNP9FRUN.markdown:
# Generative AI used to copy and clone French news media in French-speaking Africa

**Fake radio broadcasts created with artificial intelligence are gradually making their way into the arsenal of those who disinform. Whether deepfakes of journalists or just synthesised voices, AI is being used to simulate the content of well-known and trusted media in order to manipulate the public. Reporters Without Borders (RSF) is concerned about this growing disinformation trend, which no technical or legal barriers are currently able to contain.**

On 20 May, the French international news broadcaster *Radio France Internationale (RFI)* reported that it had again been the[  victim of identity theft](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/monde/20250520-infox-au-cameroun-la-notori%C3%A9t%C3%A9-de-rfi-utilis%C3%A9e-%C3%A0-des-fins-politiques) using generative AI. In a video bearing 

*RFI*’s logo, fake voices discussed Cameroonian opposition leader Maurice Kamto’s possible presidential candidacy for more than five minutes. The admissibility of his candidacy in next October’s presidential election is currently a matter of debate in political circles in Cameroon.

The dialogue in the video is laborious, the tone is crudely robotic and the format does not conform to *RFI*’s editorial practices. But RSF has learned that this is not preventing social media userss from commenting on it and circulating as if it were authentic, or WhatsApp groups from sharing it.

This is not the first time generative AI has been used in an attempt to fabricate content produced by *RFI* or other French public broadcasters. In the Democratic Republic of Congo in April, a fake radio news programme simulated the voices of **Arthur Ponchelet **(of *RFI*) and **Aurélie Bazzara** (of *France 24*) to lend credence to a public apology supposedly made by Corneille Nangaa, the leader of the AFC/M23 rebel coalition that is[  active](https://rsf.org/en/drc-m23-tightens-its-grip-local-media-north-and-south-kivu) in the provinces of South and North Kivu.

Again, the content did not appear to be generated by AI and was shared on WhatsApp, YouTube, TikTok and Facebook, accumulating more than 100,000 views. In February, f[ ake synthetic audio content](https://lesoleil.sn/web-tv/soleil-tv/soleil-check-alerte-deepfake-laudio-viral-attribue-a-rfi-et-france-24-est-un-faux/) attributed to the same two public media outlets was also widely shared on Senegalese social media.

*“Appropriating a media outlet's identity to produce fake news is nothing new, but generative AI reinforces this strategy at a lower cost. Such content poisons public debate by opening the way to an era of constant doubt, further eroding trust in the media. Generative AI platforms and tools need to incorporate concrete measures for tracking and authenticating content, in order to determine whether it is the product of a media outlet, whether it is generated by AI, or whether the necessary information is lacking. All stakeholders in the production and distribution chain, and especially content distribution platforms, must accept that they have a duty to suppress this threat.*

**Need to know where online content comes from**

 Last year, some digital companies undertook to[  report synthetic content](https://rsf.org/en/tech-giants-commit-identifying-ai-generated-content-step-forward-right-online-information-last) but such undertakings are still limited to cases where metadata is available – a constraint that is too easy to circumvent. As long as the nature of content (authentic, synthetic or of uncertain origin) remains hidden from users and is not integrated into algorithmic amplification procedures, manipulation will be able to continue and grow without restraint. 

It is becoming essential to classify publicly accessible content according to its nature – authentic and produced by journalists or the public, synthetic, or impossible to identify. It is in the absence of any clarity concerning this last category that attacks against journalists and media outlets based on deepfakes or synthetic voices are able to flourish. For the time being, the means to protect against such attacks are limited.

In 2023, the[  Paris Charter on AI and Journalism](https://rsf.org/en/rsf-and-16-partners-unveil-paris-charter-ai-and-journalism) – initiated by RSF and written by a team of experts chaired by Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Ressa – called on media outlets to adopt technology for authenticating content so that the public could be confident that it was genuine.

Such technology is currently under development and is being tested by news websites and news agencies such as *Agence France-Presse (AFP)*. These efforts must be recognised, supported and promoted by distribution platforms. Deepfakes and media identity theft can only be combated effectively if these media efforts are complemented by increased transparency on platforms.

HIMKPTNY.title: Denmark: Damaging Deepfakes Target TV Host Divya Das
HIMKPTNY.markdown:
# Denmark: Damaging Deepfakes Target TV Host Divya Das

#### Women Press Freedom condemns exploitation of journalist’s image, demands immediate action from social media platforms

`Location: Denmark``Date: April 3, 2024`Women Press Freedom vehemently condemns the exploitation of TV 2 presenter Divya Das’s image through deepfake technology. Das’ situation is part of an alarming trend Women Press Freedom has [documented](https://www.womeninjournalism.org/test#gsc.tab=0&gsc.q=deepfake%20ai&gsc.sort=): a disturbing increase in the manipulation of journalists' likenesses to spread misinformation and fraudulent content, severely undermining trust in media and endangering public discourse. The situation appears to be worsening. In just the first quarter of 2024, we documented as many deepfake cases as we did in the entirety of 2023. The misuse of Divya Das's identity for malicious purposes shows the pressing need for strong protections against deepfake technology. Women Press Freedom supports the legal action taken by TV 2. Deepfake technology poses a threat to press freedom by allowing hostile actors to fabricate convincing falsehoods, potentially tarnishing the reputation of journalists and media outlets. Social media platforms must take accountability and safeguard their users from nefarious AI manipulations.

On April 3, 2024, an investigation by outlets TjekDet and Politiken [reported](https://www.tjekdet.dk/indsigt/svindel-med-kendte-eksploderer-paa-facebook) that AI-generated images of TV 2 host Divya Das were being used without permission to promote fake news articles. These articles were tricking people into investing in fake cryptocurrency schemes. The false stories spread mainly on Facebook and Instagram, both owned by Meta.

The expose [revealed](https://www.mapmf.org/alert/31449) that Divya Das had been repeatedly targeted by deepfake technology since the beginning of the year. The latest incident involved a fake image showing Das with a black eye or red marks on her face. This manipulated image was accompanied by a false story suggesting domestic abuse, wrongly implicating Das's husband, DR TV host Kim Bildsøe Lassen. The made-up narrative claimed that Lassen had been violent after discovering undisclosed secrets.

In February, Das [said](https://www.instagram.com/p/C3qaeq_MwFZ/?hl=fr) scammers were using her image without permission on Instagram to promote fake campaigns. She warned her followers to be careful and not to believe any fabricated stories or scams circulating under her name. These scams falsely claim she's endorsing risky investment schemes, falsely attributed to reputable news portal BT.

Following the revelations, on April 19, 2024, TV 2, DR, and news portal BT collectively addressed Meta through a joint letter, urging the platform to assume accountability for defamatory and harmful content proliferation.

TV 2's managing director, Anne Engdal Stig Christensen, [announced](https://www.seoghoer.dk/kendte/tv-2-politianmelder-meta-som-ejer-facebook-efter-et-hav-af-falske-artikler-paa-mediet) the channel was initiating legal action against Meta. TV 2 has filed fraud charges, and media outlet DR is pursuing defamation charges. Law enforcement is investigating the alleged offenses.

So far this year, Women Press Freedom has documented seven cases of AI deepfake technology targeting women journalists. Their images have been manipulated to create [pornographic content](https://www.womeninjournalism.org/threats-all/uk-women-press-freedom-condemns-deepfake-attacks-on-cathy-newman-as-part-of-a-growing-trend-against-journalists) and [shill suspect investments](https://www.womeninjournalism.org/threats-all/ireland-colette-fitzpatrick-targeted-in-deepfake-scam-ad); their voices have been manipulated to [spread lies](https://www.womeninjournalism.org/threats-all/germany-demonstrators-target-susanne-daubner-and-tagesschau-journalists-with-deepfake-audio) and undermine credible news outlets.

Women Press Freedom denounces attempts to tarnish Divya Das’ reputation through AI-manipulated deepfakes. The misuse of Das's image to spread fake news shows how easily misinformation can be disseminated, eroding trust in media and endangering public discourse. The media outlets’ legal action against Meta suggests a growing recognition of the need for regulatory measures to hold platforms accountable for their role in facilitating the spread of misinformation and protecting journalists from exploitation.

Women Press Freedom supports Divya Das and outlets TV 2 and BT’s quest for legal recourse against Meta. There's a clear need for robust safeguards against deepfake technology and fraudulent activities online, including measures to verify the authenticity of content and protect individuals' identities from exploitation. We advocate for social media platforms to enact more stringent measures to combat such egregious violations of press freedom and personal dignity.

*Women Press Freedom is an initiative by The Coalition For Women In Journalism*

*The Coalition For Women In Journalism is a global organization of support for women journalists. The CFWIJ pioneered mentorship for mid-career women journalists across several countries around the world and is the first organization to focus on the status of free press for women journalists. We thoroughly document cases of any form of abuse against women in any part of the globe. Our system of individuals and organizations brings together the experience and mentorship necessary to help female career journalists navigate the industry. Our goal is to help develop a strong mechanism where women journalists can work safely and thrive.*

GYG46W9Q.title: Scammers use Al Roker's image in a recent deepfake video — how to know what's real
GYG46W9Q.markdown:
[TODAY's Al Roker](https://www.today.com/life/al-roker-a-team-morning-routine-today-show-rcna193125) got a message from a friend with a link to a video of himself promoting a solution to hypertension, or high blood pressure.

The problem is that Al doesn't have hypertension — and the video was fake.

"A friend of mine sent me a link and said, 'Is this real?'" Al told TODAY's senior investigative consumer correspondent Vicky Nguyen. "And I clicked on it, and all of a sudden, I see and hear myself talking about having a couple of heart attacks."

Al's image was [used in a deepfake](https://www.today.com/popculture/news/what-is-a-deepfake-ai-trend-rcna118993), or a video that uses artificial intelligence to doctor video and audio that appears to be real. Scammers use these deepfakes to deceive people into giving up their money.

Al emphasized he does not have hypertension, nor has he ever had a heart attack.

"It looks like me! I mean, I can tell that it’s not me ... but to the casual viewer, Al Roker's touting this hypertension cure," Al said.

"I’ve had some celebrity friends call because their parents got taken in by it," he added.

Meta, the parent company of Facebook, said it had "removed this page for violating our policies" after TODAY reached out about the deepfake post of Al.

It’s unclear who was behind the fake video of Al, but he isn't alone. A deepfake of [Taylor Swift appearing to sell](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/taylor-swift-ai-generated-le-creuset-ad-not-real-rcna133285) Le Creuset cookware sets began circulating early last year, and other celebrities like Oprah Winfrey and [Tom Hanks have spoken out](https://www.instagram.com/p/Cx2MsH9rt7q/) about fake endorsement scams using their images.

“I have nothing to do with weight loss gummies or diet pills,” [Winfrey said in 2022](https://www.instagram.com/p/CkW2EQ1Jwwo/) after a doctored video of herself started spreading online.

Imposter scams were the top fraud complaint in 2024, according to the [Federal Trade Commission](https://public.tableau.com/app/profile/federal.trade.commission/viz/TheBigViewAllSentinelReports/TopReports), with people losing more than $2.9 billion that year through the schemes.

Yoav Keren, CEO of BrandShield, a company protecting brands and public figures from imposter scams, said on TODAY the average consumer doesn't understand how easy it is to make these types of fake videos.

"I think this is becoming one of the biggest problems worldwide online," Keren said.

Al called the rise of deepfake technology "frightening."

"We used to say, 'Seeing is believing.' Well, that’s kind of out the window now," Al said.

### What can you do to stay safe from deepfake scams?

Vicky Nguyen shared some tips to help you stay safe from these types of scams online.

- Slow down. Take a moment to really look at the video to see if anything appears off, like the lip sync.
- Before buying anything, do an internet search to see what other people are saying.
- Be cautious when clicking on any social media ad links.

NLJSHHWB.title: Microsoft's robot editor confuses mixed-race Little Mix singers
NLJSHHWB.markdown:
Microsoft’s decision to replace human journalists with robots has backfired, after the tech company’s artificial intelligence software illustrated a news story about racism with a photo of the wrong mixed-race member of the [band Little Mix](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2019/sep/08/little-mixs-jesy-nelson-on-surviving-the-trolls-people-were-saying-horrific-things).

A week after [the Guardian revealed plans to fire the human editors](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2020/may/30/microsoft-sacks-journalists-to-replace-them-with-robots) who run MSN.com and replace them with Microsoft’s artificial intelligence code, an early rollout of the software resulted in a story about the [singer Jade Thirlwall](https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2020/jan/11/celebritiy-lookalikes-jade-thirlwall-bridget-christie-frank-skinner-ben-miller-rylan-clark-neal)’s [personal reflections on racism](https://www.independent.co.uk/life-style/jade-thirlwall-little-mix-race-bbc-sounds-podcast-a9543711.html) being illustrated with a picture of her fellow band member Leigh-Anne Pinnock.

Thirlwall, who attended a recent Black Lives Matter protest in London, criticised MSN on Friday, saying she was sick of “ignorant” media making such mistakes. She posted on Instagram: “@MSN If you’re going to copy and paste articles from other accurate media outlets, you might want to make sure you’re using an image of the correct mixed race member of the group.”

“This shit happens to @leighannepinnock and I ALL THE TIME that it’s become a running joke,” she said. “It offends me that you couldn’t differentiate the two women of colour out of four members of a group … DO BETTER!”

What Thirlwall could not have known, according to sources at the company, is that the image was selected by Microsoft’s artificial intelligence software, which is already responsible for editing parts of the news site, which attracts hundreds of millions of readers worldwide.

Microsoft does not carry out original reporting but employs human editors to select, edit and repurpose articles from news outlets, including the Guardian. Articles are then hosted on Microsoft’s website and the tech company shares advertising revenue with the original publishers. At the end of last month, Microsoft decided to fire hundreds of journalists in the middle of a pandemic and fully replace them with the artificial intelligence software.

Asked why Microsoft was deploying software that cannot tell mixed-race individuals apart, whether apparent racist bias could seep into deployments of the company’s artificial intelligence software by leading corporations, and whether the company would reconsider plans to replace the human editors with robots, a spokesman for the tech company said: “As soon as we became aware of this issue, we immediately took action to resolve it and have replaced the incorrect image.”

In advance of the publication of this article, staff at MSN were told to expect a negative article in the Guardian about alleged racist bias in the artificial intelligence software that will soon take their jobs.

Because they are unable to stop the new robot editor selecting stories from external news sites such as the Guardian, the remaining human staff have been told to stay alert and delete a version of this article if the robot decides it is of interest and automatically publishes it on MSN.com. They have also been warned that even if they delete it, the robot editor may overrule them and attempt to publish it again.

Staff have already had to delete coverage criticising MSN for running the story about [Little Mix](https://www.theguardian.com/music/little-mix) with the wrong image after the AI software decided stories about the incident would interest MSN readers.

One staff member said Microsoft was deeply concerned about reputational damage to its AI product: “With all the anti-racism protests at the moment, now is not the time to be making mistakes.”

8GEKEU5X.title: The Tiny Israeli Start-Up Behind Hundreds of AI Pink Slime News Sites
8GEKEU5X.markdown:
**Update 8/17/26: **[Prism News’ websites](https://www.prismnews.com/) are all down and displaying this message: **“We have currently completed our initial experiment. A big thank you to all who participated and gave their feedback. All activity is suspended for the foreseeable future.”**

**Update 8/14/26:** [Part 2 of Spin Class’ investigation into Prism News is live here](https://spinclass.substack.com/p/i-try-to-assume-stupidity-instead). Shortly after we reached out to Flex Capital, Prism’s main VC backer, for comment, all of Prism’s website content went offline, with individual Prism homepages displaying the message “Under Maintenance.”

In July, Interlochen Public Radio reporter Maxwell Howard [ran a story](https://www.interlochenpublicradio.org/ipr-news/2026-07-16/michigans-newest-newsrooms-are-ai-machines-built-on-others-reporting) on a mysterious Northern Michigan newsroom that seemingly popped up overnight. What it uncovered was a digital news Westworld: where AI “journalists” produce real-sounding local news, scraped from actual reporting, and repackage it as a shiny new product— but laden with clunky Frankenstein-ed text, dangerous hallucinations, and what one journalist described to Spin Class as “a theft of our work.”

IPR had stumbled on a single node of a network: around 200 AI-powered websites, powered by a four-person Israeli tech start-up called [Prism News](https://www.prismnews.com/). A new flavor of classic pink slime journalism.

[Launched in May 2026](https://www.newsfilecorp.com/release/298739), Prism News is a private digital media company headquartered in Tel Aviv. Its co-founders are tech entrepreneurs, not journalists, and the quality of Prism’s output reflects that origin. More on them in Part 2 next week: for now, Part 1 explores how Prism is evolving the pink slime model, how it works in practice, and the impacts Prism is already having across some communities. 

### “I don’t really see a compelling product”

Prism’s arrival signals a new chapter in pink slime journalism across the U.S.[1](https://spinclass.substack.com#footnote-1) The experts I interviewed agreed Prism seems to be the first major example of a foreign tech startup running a U.S. local news network at scale — itself potentially a huge new development, even minus the AI aspects. Prism’s pink slime is [backed by VC funding](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/1356596-29#overview), which presumably means Prism’s leadership convinced somebody that this tiny Israeli start-up is the first company to ever crack making local news profitable. And, at least so far, Prism content generally eschews the hyper-partisan, right-wing sensationalism that animates most U.S. pink slime.

Perhaps most interestingly, [Prism openly touts that the whole endeavor is AI-powered](https://finance.yahoo.com/sectors/technology/articles/prism-media-launches-prism-news-110700659.html?guccounter=1&guce_referrer=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZ29vZ2xlLmNvbS8&guce_referrer_sig=AQAAABjLGCSDve8m0M_iF32Y-ijoCMM5cHU7MoI3FryF4bVG22fIsstFBhrB_J8_zeDXsh7Rm880CXbUkTDXVbklyJ5wQ8_YcZCVBm-K9Mwv6R--dQF4a3AWUqHA6_5ONsVW47Tw_jTY2ef5Y89t_jJ387OG3RU5oXxNCe1IZ5aSe3Bu) (at least in its marketing materials, though not so much on individual stories; more on that later). We’re in a moment where publishers are suing AI giants for using news reporting as unlicensed training data, major movie studios are suing AI-image companies for IP theft, and seemingly every writer is ferociously debating what constitutes appropriate uses of AI in journalism. Yet Prism and its backers decided now was the right moment to build a massive AI-powered network of virtual local newsrooms.

“The idea of AI-powered news is generally attractive to the Silicon Valley types” MediaWise director and Poynter Institute faculty member Alex Mahadevan told me in an interview. “If you've been to any journalism conference in the past two years, you’ve heard about the idea of news reporting and investigative reporting as basically the first layer of the news experience, which then is outsourced to AI: repackaging things as chatbots, as articles, as videos, etc.”

However, “when I look at Prism, I don’t really see a compelling product,” Mahadevan continued. “I see a defective product that, for the most part, is duplicating efforts from actual reporting that already exists. The images are poor. The layout is really poor. It’s not a very inviting user experience.”

“When I hear that there’s VC money flowing into this,” he added, “it’s insane to me to put money into [this] and expect any sort of ROI.”

So if Prism isn’t a very compelling product, why cover it? Why does yet another AI slop project matter in the grand scheme of things?

 “The U.S. has lost nearly 3,500 local newspapers since 2005 - almost 40% of the country’s total,” declared the May 2026 [press release](https://finance.yahoo.com/sectors/technology/articles/prism-media-launches-prism-news-110700659.html?guccounter=1&guce_referrer=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZ29vZ2xlLmNvbS8&guce_referrer_sig=AQAAABjLGCSDve8m0M_iF32Y-ijoCMM5cHU7MoI3FryF4bVG22fIsstFBhrB_J8_zeDXsh7Rm880CXbUkTDXVbklyJ5wQ8_YcZCVBm-K9Mwv6R--dQF4a3AWUqHA6_5ONsVW47Tw_jTY2ef5Y89t_jJ387OG3RU5oXxNCe1IZ5aSe3Bu) announcing Prism News. “Roughly 50 million Americans live in what researchers call a news desert. Prism Media was built to address that gap.”

Prism got the diagnosis right: the collapse of local news outlets is a real crisis for U.S. journalism (and democracy). But is Prism’s model really the right way to fill this void?

How will audiences react to realizing that the “reporter” behind the news they see on Facebook or Nextdoor is actually a foreign-owned chatbot? How does more AI slop help rebuild audience trust in journalism, when all evidence seems to signal the opposite effect? And how will real, struggling news outlets compete with floods of AI pink slime? If a local newsroom loses clicks and ad revenue to an AI company that scraped and repurposed its journalism, how does that impact their community?

I sent Prism a long list of these and other questions, most of which they did not answer. But a Prism spokesman provided a number of statements defending their operations, which I’ve included throughout. As best I can tell, these are by far the most detailed comments Prism has given on the record.

### The Fake AI Reporter Telling You How to Avoid a Measles Outbreak

“Several of your questions appear to assume that we copy and republish articles,” Prism’s Head of Growth Partnerships Daniel Koren told me in an email. “That is not how our system works. Instead, we use licensed AI search tools together with publicly available facts and data to gather factual information about stories from multiple independent sources. Our system then synthesizes and transforms those facts into a completely new article, written from scratch, often with additional context, a different structure, and a different editorial angle based on what the system determines would be most useful for readers.”

What’s missing in Prism’s explanation: any mention of licensing content, seeking publisher or journalist permission, or sharing ad revenue or other compensation with the reporters whose work Prism acknowledges it pulls from.

Those “different editorial angles” are bylined by one of [around 40 AI Prism “reporters”](https://www.prismnews.com/journalists) who supposedly cover everything from local politics to jewelry (two reporters on that last beat - who says journalism is dying?). One “reporter,” [Dr. Elena Rodriguez](https://www.prismnews.com/journalists/elena-rodriguez), bylines her articles with her PhD title:

“Dr. Rodriguez,” of course, is not real. None of Prism’s reporters are real. I asked Prism what they were trying to achieve with these AI journalists: why give an AI-written article a byline, fake credentials, and a made-up backstory rather than simply disclosing that content is AI-generated? Were they worried that audiences might feel misled by fake biographies of people who aren’t actually real?

Take “Dr. Rodriguez” and her recent [“report” about a measles outbreak among Arizona farmworkers](https://www.prismnews.com/local/fresno-ca/fresno-county-monitors-farmworkers-exposed-to-measles-in). Prism’s article notes what CDC and local public health websites say, lists symptoms to watch for, and describes how measles may have been transmitted among farm workers. But just because something looks and feels real doesn’t mean it *is* real: there are no quotes, no links, no actual citations, no interviews, no original reporting in Prism’s story on the outbreak. And the whole thing is “authored” by a foreign tech company cosplaying as an American local reporter/doctor, delivering public health advice. 

If Prism’s AI were to misrepresent real public health information, or to hallucinate something entirely, and publish the result under a byline with “Dr.” in it, how would readers know to be skeptical? And who would be responsible for any real-world harm caused? What if any recourse would audiences have?

Prism did not answer those questions directly, but insisted, “Next to each name/profile there is an ‘AI’ mark that is clickable that links directly to additional and specific information explaining that they are AI personas and how they are used on the platform etc.”

The above screen grabs do have these small “AI” badges that link to [Prism’s AI disclosure page](https://www.prismnews.com/disclaimer). But there don’t appear to be any such AI disclosures on Prism’s social media accounts, even though social media is a key driver for local news traffic:

The articles these fake journalists supposedly byline aren’t original reporting: they are AI-scrapes of real journalists’ work, among other online sources. And the quality of the repurposed news stories Prism pumps out leaves a lot to be desired.

AI-powered pink slime isn’t just a bad user experience (though it’s also that). Prism’s AI makes significant mistakes. [As IPR reported,](https://www.interlochenpublicradio.org/ipr-news/2026-07-16/michigans-newest-newsrooms-are-ai-machines-built-on-others-reporting) Prism has hallucinated fake images of real people, including making them the wrong race:

Prism also de-contextualizes facts to the point of misinformation (more on that in a bit). And it makes serious errors in judgement that a real reporter would never make— including, I was alarmed to learn, naming a real underage abuse victim in an article it scraped from a legitimate local news outlet.

### Fake Reporter, Real Victim’s Real Name

Earlier this summer, Prism scraped [an IPR story](https://www.interlochenpublicradio.org/ipr-news/2026-05-27/mother-says-grand-traverse-court-sent-son-to-missouri-facility-despite-abuse-concerns) featuring an interview with a parent whose teenage child was sent to a residential facility beset by over a decade’s-worth of sexual and physical abuse allegations. While at the facility, her child was attacked by another resident, said he was verbally threatened by staff, and given marijuana by another staff member.

IPR ran all this in their story, while withholding the minor’s name. **But, IPR told me, the AI-generated Prism article somehow published with the real, unredacted name of the underage victim.** It was only after IPR contacted Prism that the minor’s name was removed from the Prism story, without any further acknowledgement or explanation.

Howard told me his best guess was that Prism’s AI tool was able to correctly ID the minor from other public sources like local government records, but that there was no way to know for sure. Prism declined to answer questions about how the minor’s name was initially included, who was responsible, and what steps, if any, Prism took to keep it from happening again.

“Like every business, we occasionally make mistakes,” Prism’s Koren wrote, “and when we become aware of them, we correct them.” But Prism wouldn’t say how it becomes aware of mistakes, or how either its AI or human staff verifies the accuracy of its content. I asked Prism whether it was the responsibility of the outlets whose content Prism scrapes to contact them with any errors, even serious ones like naming an underage abuse victim, but Prism did not respond.

“The advantage of an AI-native workflow,” Koren continued, “is that every solution for an issue can immediately become a permanent improvement to the system. Rather than relying solely on individual judgment, we continuously add validation layers and quality checks that reduce the likelihood of similar issues happening again.”

Part of the trouble with this argument is that Prism isn’t removing individual judgment: it’s removing *human *judgment. Anyone can configure an AI agent to follow a code of conduct, or change steps to its workflow (though there’s no promise that the AI would actually follow those directions). But Prism seems to be betting that enough workflow adjustments can match an experienced journalist’s judgement, even around the kind of sensitive stories that would never be featured in a press release.

Alas, even the most sophisticated AI can’t build genuine trust with a source who has never told their story and fears speaking up. AI doesn’t live in the same community as its subjects, facing them in the grocery store or at school pick-up. AI can’t feel a reporter’s determination to cover their stories with care, honesty, and fairness because AI, by definition, doesn’t feel.

“The flaws here are beyond factuality and AI slop,” IPR’s Howard told me. “AI doesn’t have the heart of a person thinking about how a story is told, and what their responsibility is to the people in it.”

If anything, an AI company headquartered overseas but purporting to cover local U.S. communities is whole other level of disconnected from the people in its “articles.” How can a four-person tech start-up in Tel Aviv credibly claim to vouch for what is happening on the ground in Traverse City, or Baltimore, or Albuquerque (all areas with solid local media environments, for what it’s worth)? How can tech workers who have never worked as journalists, reported a story from start to finish, or even interviewed a source, be trusted to oversee AI that purports to be genuine U.S. local news, and pumps out hundreds of articles daily about real people, places, and controversies?

I asked Prism all these questions. They did not provide any answers.

### Prism Pitched A Journalist His Own AI-Rewritten Reporting

[Allan Leibowitz](https://muckrack.com/allan-leibowitz/bio) is an award-winning Australian journalist who has run an electronic percussion news site called [digitalDrummer](https://digitaldrummermag.com/2026/07/25/digitaldrummer-calls-out-ai-content-scraping/) since 2010. Leibowitz[ wrote on Substack](https://digitaldrummer.substack.com/p/when-ai-becomes-the-expert) that he first became aware of Prism when he received an email from Daniel Koren** pitching Leibowitz back his own repurposed content**. Leibowitz later shared that email with me:

*We recently featured digitalDrummer on Prism News in a piece titled “digitalDrummer defends latency tests as electronic kits get faster.”*

*You can read it here:*

*[link]*

*Thought you might enjoy seeing it. If you think your community would enjoy it too, we’d really appreciate it if you shared it.*

**“The irony,” Leibowitz later told me, “was that I was being asked to promote to my own readers an AI-generated reworking of my own article.”**

When Leibowitz started investigating Prism, he was alarmed to find that this was not an isolated incident. “Our review,” [he later wrote](https://digitaldrummermag.com/2026/07/25/digitaldrummer-calls-out-ai-content-scraping/), “found that Prism News published corresponding articles for eight of the 10 stories digitalDrummer published between June 10 and July 15, 2026. Those articles included not only routine product announcements, but also original interviews, contributed articles and proprietary testing that originated with digitalDrummer.”

This pattern of regularly appropriating another journalist’s work is concerning enough. But Leibowitz also noted that Prism articles drawing on his work frequently distorted his original reporting. The article Prism pitched back to Leibowitz was one of these. “It reached conclusions we had not made,” Leibowitz told me, “and used latency measurements from an outdated version of our results table to identify the fastest and slowest drum modules. Those rankings were no longer accurate.”

“More fundamentally,” he added, “‘the author’ did not appear to understand the significance or limitations of the testing. digitalDrummer has been independently measuring drum-module latency for well over a decade, and these are figures manufacturers generally don’t publish.”

You don’t have to be an electronic drumming expert, or publish a niche hobbyist outlet, to see the implications of AI scraping and regurgitating material, distorting it to the point of inaccuracy, and then pushing it out at a scale and speed that no human-run media operation can match.

“The potential impact for a small specialist publisher is obvious,” Leibowitz told me. “We invest the time and money in finding stories, interviewing people, testing products and building expertise; another site can then generate competing content almost immediately, potentially competing for the same search traffic, readers and advertising without making that investment.”

“I welcome additional coverage of electronic percussion,” Leibowitz added. “But there’s an enormous difference between another journalist independently covering the same subject and an automated publishing system using our output as the raw material for its own coverage.”

Writers have always competed for scoops. And yes, sometimes they borrow ideas, words, even wholesale texts from each other without giving proper credit. What makes Prism different is the speed, scale, and automation of that borrowing— and that systematic scraping and AI repackaging of human journalists’ work is now a VC-backed business model.

“All I can say,” Leibowitz ruefully concluded, “is thank goodness this is happening at the end of my career rather than at the start.”

### “Employee and Workplace News”

Prism’s third vertical, “Employee and Workplace News,” features around 20 individual large multinational companies, including Starbucks, McDonald’s, and Goldman Sachs (also, confusingly, “[Restaurants](https://www.prismnews.com/workplace/restaurants)”). Like its other content, Prism Employee news sites largely feature AI scrapes of open-source material like press releases, marketing assets, and other legitimate (or at least human) reporting.

Prism’s description for each workplace page describes it as “a tailored magazine for [company] employees and alumni,” implying that these sites are related to the company in question. However, **a KPMG spokesperson told me that there is “no commercial relationship” between KPMG US and Prism News. They were unaware of the site and Prism News generally, he added, before Spin Class contacted them.**

As with its “local news” and hobbyist content, Prism’s workplace articles are bylined by AI reporters, not real people. And, as with other Prism articles, the AI-generated workplace content is an unpleasant and often confusing reading experience.

Take [this article about pay transparency in restaurants,](https://www.prismnews.com/workplace/restaurants/restaurant-pay-transparency-rules-push-hiring-disclosures) seemingly cobbled from several different sources: I’ve read it three times, yet truly cannot tell you what it says. Names appear with no explanation of who the person is, or why they are in the story. There are no links to any of the supposed studies or sources cited. One of the sections is headed “*Pay transparency is no longer just an HR slogan–*” which, tell me you’ve never worked in a restaurant without telling me you’ve never worked in a restaurant.

“Some of our publications are created by users around communities or interests they care about,” Prism’s Koren told me via email. “For example, a Monday.com alumnus can create a publication focused on topics that may be relevant to other alumni.” Prism CEO Dekel Valtzer previously worked at both [Monday.com](http://monday.com/) and KPMG, according to [his LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dekelvaltzer/).

Prism News declined to answer whether any of the other companies listed in its Employee and Workplace News section have partnership agreements or other contractual arrangements with Prism. It also declined to comment on how its partnership model works.

The experts I talked to were cautious about whether Prism’s use of these companies’ IP might be a legal vulnerability for the company. Moreover, the question might be less about legality and more about resources and priorities for those companies. “It takes time and resources to send the takedown request, or file lawsuits for copyright infringement,” Mahadevan told me, also adding that a multinational company would likely be better positioned to take on such a fight than a struggling local newsroom.

### “A complete reinvention of how humanity stays informed.”

I’ve had plenty of [frustration with AI slop content](https://spinclass.substack.com/p/ai-slop-resistance-grift-and-embracing), how [AI companies’ PR and policy mistakes have inadvertently deepened many audiences’ trust in AI](https://spinclass.substack.com/p/the-pr-backlash-to-big-techs-villain), and [platforms struggling to adopt coherent AI policies](https://substack.com/@emilyhorne/note/c-300148597?r=3yovfp&utm_source=notes-share-action&utm_medium=web). That said, I don’t find blanket screeds against AI, or even AI in journalism, especially useful or interesting. These technologies aren’t going anywhere, nor is the money behind them: genie, bottle, etc.

Instead, I’m much more interested in messy questions about how we’re all adapting to this brave new world, like how struggling newsrooms are grappling with AI-powered competition. How AI disclosures impact audience trust. How AI companies frame the challenges they say they’re addressing, and whether/how they actually deliver on them. And, as always, the big Spin Class questions: *who wants me to see this? Why? Why now? What are we not talking about that we should be talking about?*

Prism has a tiny footprint today. “In reality,” Koren wrote, “the vast majority [of our sites] receive very little traffic and many have virtually no readers at all because they haven’t even been indexed by Google yet. Again, this reflects the stage we’re currently at as a very young startup.”

Still, Prism’s marketing materials tout big ambitions. [From their homepage](https://www.prismnews.com/):

Start-up culture is littered with the tombstones of companies that promised investors they’d change humanity, only to burn through their start-up capital and flame out. But it’s worth taking Prism’s intentions seriously, especially given the ease with which a small start-up can vibe-code a digital news empire. When I asked Alex Mahadevan at Poynter how long it would take him to build a Prism-size pink slime network he paused, and mused, “maybe a day?”

Still, it’s hard to imagine a Prism-like AI news network actually replacing real journalism entirely, if for no other reason than it needs content to scrape. AI, as Allan Leibowitz [wrote,](https://digitaldrummer.substack.com/p/when-ai-becomes-the-expert) “can’t discover something that isn’t already on the web.” 

Yet Prism’s stated vision forces us to ask: “what the world would look like if humans were cut out of journalism entirely?” Because that seems to be the future that Prism and its backers are betting on.

More of that next week in Part 2.

*Huge thank you to Maxwell Howard at Interlochen Public Radio, whose intrepid reporting sparked this story. You can  support IPR here, and become a paid Spin Class subscriber here - these kinds of stories take a long time to report, and your subscriptions make a huge difference! *

[1](https://spinclass.substack.com#footnote-anchor-1)

Refresher from Spin Class’ February[ investigation of a different pink slime network](https://spinclass.substack.com/p/spin-class-case-study-i-caught-politico): “Pink slime” journalism describes outlets that publish poor quality reports, frequently automated, that appear to be local news. As of 2024 there are [more pink slime fake news websites in the U.S. than there are local news outlets.](https://www.newsnationnow.com/business/tech/fake-news-sites-outnumber-us-newspaper-sites/#:~:text=Your%20Money,abortion%20lead%20their%20ballot:%20Poll)

"Still, it’s hard to imagine a Prism-like AI news network actually replacing real journalism entirely, if for no other reason than it needs content to scrape. AI, as Allan Leibowitz wrote, 'can’t discover something that isn’t already on the web.'"

Seems like the obvious (terrible) outcome is that AIs will scrape other AI stories, in an endless recursive bullshit loop that will further and further distort reality.

595GWMQH.title: Royal cleaner stories removed by Times and Sun after authenticity questions
595GWMQH.markdown:
Stories featuring a ‘royal cleaner’ who claimed to have worked for the Royal Family for more than a decade have been withdrawn after questions were raised by Press Gazette about their authenticity.

Interviews with ‘Anne Simmons’ featured in dozens of stories from major newspaper publishers this year, including the [Daily Mail](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/home/you/article-14523871/A-royal-housekeeper-reveals-three-supermarket-essentials-used-spring-clean-Buckingham-Palace-bathrooms-one-just-35p.html), [Daily Express](https://www.express.co.uk/life-style/property/2057090/cleaner-Buckingham-Palace-hoover-alternative-slime), [The Sun](https://www.the-sun.com/royals/13813313/buckingham-palace-trick-fluffy-towels-avoid-musty-smells/), [New York Post](https://nypost.com/2025/05/14/entertainment/king-charles-has-banned-two-household-items-from-buckingham-palace/) and [Daily Mirror](https://www.mirror.co.uk/lifestyle/food-drink/royal-cleaning-expert-shares-10-35293603) as well as many regional titles and blogs. 

The pieces offered insights into everything from the items Prince Charles would not permit in Palace bathrooms to Kate Middleton’s morning routine.

The Times (in a [now-removed piece](https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/property-home/article/how-do-you-spruce-up-buckingham-palace-a-royal-cleaner-spills-h3sl6cz3t) which can still be seen on [archive sites](https://archive.ph/PwKoW#selection-1721.42-1721.56)) appeared to run with the story first, on 5 March 2025, with subsequent bursts of coverage across the media in April and May.

The Sun and Times (both part of News UK) removed articles about Simmons after Press Gazette asked questions about their authenticity.

The later pieces centre around ‘tip-style’ content such as how Buckingham Palace uses vinegar instead of fabric softener, and items allegedly banned by Prince Charles in Buckingham Palace, including wet wipes and scented candles.

Coverage appears to have been based on press releases sent out on behalf of a number of companies that claimed to have interviewed Simmons including: Edit Suits, Plumbworld, Playcasino, Plates Express and Pure Window Cleaning.

In the initial Times story, Simmons was described as a “brand ambassador” for Hyperion Tiles.

As far as Press Gazette can ascertain, there is no record of anyone called ‘Anne Simmons’ having worked for Buckingham Palace, either as staff or an outside contractor.

There is also no record of her being vetted for security, which would have happened had she worked in Buckingham Palace.

Had she worked for the Royal Family, she would also have had to sign confidentiality agreements, and her multiple stories in newspaper publishers would breach those agreements.

All the stories feature just one image of ‘Simmons’ sitting on a sofa, and the copy in each piece seems to have been sent out via email, rather than Simmons being available for phone interview. There remains the possibility that Anne Simmons is a pseudonym, but this is not made clear in any of the copy.

Press Gazette has seen copy sent out to national newspapers with quotes from Anne Simmons promoting a company, Edit Suits, which claimed that staff at Buckingham Palace were banned from wearing onesies.

Stories sent out with links to Edit Suits include one on Princess Kate’s morning routine, which featured in the [Express](https://www.express.co.uk/news/royal/2036775/princess-kate-morning-routine), the [Mirror](https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/royals/princess-kates-surprisingly-simple-morning-34977513) and [Hello Magazine](https://www.hellomagazine.com/healthandbeauty/mother-and-baby/826638/kate-middleton-vital-solo-mornings-before-three-kids-daily-fights/) along with [Country and Town House](https://www.countryandtownhouse.com/style/health-and-beauty/kate-middleton-morning-routine/).

Most of the pieces featuring Simmons featured prominent links to Plumbworld, a plumbing company which was [linked last week](https://pressgazette.co.uk/news/agencies-linked-to-missing-lottery-winners-bombard-journalists-with-fake-case-studies-ai/?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email) to PR agencies Signal the News and Relay the Update, which have been bombarding journalists with press releases featuring seemingly fake case studies in recent months.

One press release from Relay the Update featured similar ‘life hacks’ to those offered by Simmons from a chef, Daniel Harris, who is also extremely hard to find online.

The press release: “I’m a chef – here’s the £1 kitchen item I use to clean burnt pans fast”, had a 99.9% probability of containing AI writing, according to AI checker [Pangram](https://www.pangram.com/). 

Press Gazette contacted the agencies last week and this week to ask about Anne Simmons and other case studies, but got no reply.

The Simmons quotes are often presented as “interviewed by Plumbworld” or “interviewed by Edit Suits”, suggesting the stories had been sent out as a ready-made release.

In recent months, multiple hard-to-find experts linked to Plumbworld have had articles appear in the British press, seemingly sent out as campaigns to gain links in reputable sites such as newspaper publishers.

Links on newspaper sites are highly valuable because they can boost the search engine rankings of websites, helping to drive sales.

Charlotte Hughes, a wellness advisor for the company, had advice featured in [the Mirror](https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/health/simple-shower-hack-can-relieve-34080309), [Surrey Live](https://www.getsurrey.co.uk/news/health/wellness-advisor-says-bathroom-trick-30341589) and [Express](https://www.express.co.uk/life-style/property/1980958/how-to-remove-limescale-bathroom) among others. 

Hughes has no profile on social media and no presence on Plumbworld’s site, and the company did not respond to requests to verify her.

Other experts with links to Plumbworld who are very hard to find online include dermatologist Dr Helena Watson, whose skincare advice has featured in the [Daily Express](https://www.express.co.uk/news/uk/2062897/unexpected-bathroom-habit-could-boost), [New York Post](https://nypost.com/2025/06/10/health/common-cooking-mistake-could-be-making-you-break-out-its-not-your-diet/), [Liverpool Echo](https://www.liverpoolecho.co.uk/news/health/experts-reveal-28p-kitchen-product-31476665) and more.

There is no trace of Dr Watson online, either on an official medical site or on social media.

The PR agencies linked to some of these case studies all have exactly the same website design, and link to Romanian companies including SIV Media.

The websites do not appear to be fully finished, and show text saying “Buy full template”, linking to a generic template design for a PR agency.

Staff at the organisations did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Challenged to prove that Anne Simmons existed, Plumbworld made no response over several days to requests sent via the company’s official communications channel.

The company’s CEO and its marketing chief also did not respond to requests sent both via email and via LinkedIn.

Press Gazette reached out to Edit Suits for comment via Linkedin and email and has not heard anything.

Stories on both The Times (which featured an ‘interview’ with Simmons in its Homes and Property section in March this year, where ‘Simmons’ revealed that Buckingham Palace would have a deep clean in advance of Donald Trump’s visit) and multiple stories on sister News UK title The Sun have now been deleted online.

Publisher Reach, which featured stories from ‘Simmons’ including a “10-minute trick trick for clean taps under £1” on sites including the Mirror and the Express, has said that it is overhauling its procedures on quoting experts in the wake of a number of suspicious ‘experts’ sent out by PR and SEO agencies.

The publisher has increased scrutiny over outside content this week in the wake of these stories.

A Reach spokesperson said: “We take the validity of our experts extremely seriously and have been working hard to weed out these fake experts.

“As these fake experts continue to proliferate, we will all need to develop more sophisticated ways to guard against this risk.

“In the meantime we will operate with a far more limited whitelist of approved experts only, which is also not ideal but necessary to stem this tide.”

Press Gazette contacted other newsbrands that published stories featuring Simmons including the Daily Mail and New York Post but has not received any comment at the time of publication.

Email ** pged@pressgazette.co.uk** to point out mistakes, provide story tips or send in a letter for publication on our "Letters Page" blog

499R57HJ.title: "I Try to Assume Stupidity Instead of Malice:" Prism Media Investigation Part 2
499R57HJ.markdown:
**Update 8/17/26: **[Prism News’ websites](https://www.prismnews.com/) are all down and displaying this message: **“We have currently completed our initial experiment. A big thank you to all who participated and gave their feedback. All activity is suspended for the foreseeable future.”**

*If you haven’t read  Part 1 of our investigation into Prism News — the VC-backed Israeli pink slime start-up — you’ll want to start there. You’ll learn about how Prism’s AI scrapes real journalism, Frankensteins it, and republishes it bylined by AI “reporters,” how Prism pitched a reporter’s own work back to him, and how they published the name of an underage abuse victim:*

*And please consider becoming a paid Spin Class subscriber to support research and reporting like this series (or you can  buy me a coffee):*

**Note: As this article was being finalized on August 13, Prism Media’s websites went down “for maintenance.” As of publication, Prism outlets have been down for over nine hours. I’ll update with any further information.**

What most intrigued me when I first started looking into [Prism News](https://www.prismnews.com/local) was not the quality of its content (pink slime has been around for years), the AI of it all (inevitable), or even that it’s an Israeli company producing US local news (definitely noteworthy, but given the AI of it all of course non-US actors would eventually get into the space). 

**What most surprised me was that a reputable VC firm had decided to go into the pink slime news business. **That’s what we’re going to unpack here. 

But first: since Part 1, some readers flagged [new reporting ](https://www.newsfromthestates.com/article/gallup-officials-respond-recent-flooding-they-say-ai-news-outlet-getting-way)about how Prism spread misinformation about crime and natural disasters in New Mexico:


Local officials said in addition to grappling with natural disasters, they were also responding to a new AI news outlet named Prism McKinley County that they say has regularly published false and misleading information in a time of crisis.

For instance, within the last week, Prism published a story about a woman drowning in floods, but the death occurred last year, according to Matt Robinson, Gallup’s tourism and marketing manager. The misleading story caused people to believe the recent floods caused her death, he said. The recent flooding has not caused any deaths or injuries, according to city officials.

“They’re taking things that happened years ago that are negative, bringing them to light, scaring people, and sharing false information,” Robinson said. “It’s really not a good thing.”

Other misleading or false stories include one July 18 that reported that two women were robbed and beaten at a Walmart. The article goes on to say that the robbery actually occurred March 3, 2020, and Police Chief Erin Toadlena-Pablo told Source NM she does not know where the outlet got its information.

Still, the article received roughly 250 shares and dozens of comments, most of which decried security concerns at the Walmart, which is one of the main grocery stores in town.

The misleading posts prompted[a Facebook post](https://www.facebook.com/photo.php?fbid=1327612289542905&set=pb.100068824406070.-2207520000&type=3)by the Gallup Police Department advising residents to use “verified sources and/or official government channels to obtain the most dependable information.”

With 200+ Prism News sites pumping out AI-generated and bylined articles daily, there are surely more examples like this floating around. But we’re going to pivot to talk about structure: where did Prism come from, the money behind it, and why this all matters — with a special guest appearance by one of the more notorious tech and media figures in recent memory.

### “We will either crash or become Amazon”

Prism would not answer my questions about why its Israeli founders got into the U.S. local news business. However, it doesn’t appear that any of their four employees have ever worked in media. Instead, per their LinkedIn profiles, they appear to come from tech start-up backgrounds.

Prism Media (Prism’s News’s parent company; we’ll use Prism Media from here on out since we’re talking about its business side) CEO Dekel Valtzer, a [former professional tennis player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dekel_Valtzer), is a tech entrepreneur and investor.
