8TZKTWS3.title: Scammers Are Creating Fake News Videos to Blackmail Victims
8TZKTWS3.markdown:
When online 

[romance](https://archive.ph/o/c037F/https://www.wired.com/2015/10/online-dating-made-woman-pawn-global-crime-plot/)and[sextortion](https://archive.ph/o/c037F/https://www.wired.com/story/jeff-bezos-sextortion-allegation/)scammers sense they’ve found a victim who may send them money, they’ll use all kinds of villainous methods to get paid. They’ll frequently stoop to blackmail—and are constantly creating more devious approaches to incorporate it into their grifts. In recent months, cybercriminals have taken their blackmailing efforts up a notch, creating realistic-looking “news” videos that claim their victims are wanted for crimes.Scammers based in West Africa, likely in Nigeria and going under the broad umbrella of the 

[Yahoo Boys](https://archive.ph/o/c037F/https://www.wired.com/story/yahoo-boys-scammers-facebook-telegram-tiktok-youtube/), have increasingly been seen sending blackmail victims videos likely using AI-generated news anchors in a bid to pressure victims into paying up. A WIRED review of posts on Telegram by self-styled Yahoo Boys shows the cybercriminals are impersonating television stations based in the US and sharing tutorials about how to create the blackmailing videos.The videos follow a sinister pattern. One video—which can be seen in the image below—uses CNN’s logo and branding to impersonate the news organization, with text at the bottom of the screen describing the “breaking news.” On the screen, a likely AI-generated newsreader starts talking.

“Good day. My name is Kristina Lawson, reporting from New Jersey,” the anchor says in the nearly minute-long clip. “Just in: we have received a credible report regarding a disturbing incident.” The fake presenter says that a “young lady” has come forward to allege that they were sexually assaulted by an older man. In the video, the man, who is the target of the scam, is named and a photograph of him appears onscreen.

Other videos seen by WIRED feature different news readers and names of news channels, but they also show more graphic photos of the potential blackmail targets, including nude and explicit images. In one “news” clip, the screen is split in two, with a photo of a man’s face on one side and the other side is a short video clip of him allegedly masturbating.

David Maimon, the head of fraud insights at SentiLink and a professor at Georgia State University who 

[first spotted](https://archive.ph/o/c037F/https://www.linkedin.com/posts/david-maimon-29343632_fraudpatrol-cnn-fraudprevention-activity-7275142958775975937-k1AD?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop)the CNN video in December, says the fraudsters have made a number of “disturbing” changes to their blackmailing tactics in recent months, including trying to humiliate people and potentially targeting those outside of English-speaking countries.Photograph Courtesy of Telegram

Typically, 

[Yahoo Boy](https://archive.ph/o/c037F/https://www.wired.com/story/nigerian-email-scammers-more-effective-than-ever/)[scammers message hundreds](https://archive.ph/o/c037F/https://www.wired.com/story/yahoo-boys-scammers-facebook-telegram-tiktok-youtube/)of people online while posing as members of the opposite sex using pictures stolen from social media profiles. They run all types of scams, but for those that involve blackmail, they often attempt to build up a relationship with their potential victim and obtain compromising information—most commonly, nude images. Then they shift gears.“At some point, they reveal their identity after they get everything that they need, and then they start blackmailing,” Maimon says. They demand money and threaten to release images online or send them to family and friends if they’re not paid. “One of the approaches they use in order to make sure that the blackmail is realistic is actually producing those news clips that they send to the victims and in a way push them, nudge them, to pay the blackmail,” he says. “They try to push you to make decisions under conditions of stress, under conditions of urgency.”

Yahoo Boy fraudsters widely use social media platform Telegram as a way of organizing, chatting with each other, and as a marketplace where they sell knowledge and tutorials about how to operate different types of scams. The “news” videos seen by WIRED appear to include the details and images of real-world victims, although it was not possible to immediately verify the cases.

Brian Mason, a constable with the Edmonton Police Service in Canada who investigates fraud and works with the victims of scams, says he has seen cases where videos or screenshots of fake CNN broadcasts have been sent to victims. “It looks like your typical CNN broadcast,” Mason says. “It's very, very convincing.” Mason says the approach has been utilized in 

[sextortion scams](https://archive.ph/o/c037F/https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/article/2024/aug/21/how-west-africas-online-fraudsters-moved-into-sextortion), which commonly target teenagers and[have been linked to a series of suicides](https://archive.ph/o/c037F/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2llzppyx05o).Mason says he has seen incidents where the news clips falsely accuse scam victims of talking with underage females and that police are searching for them or have issued warrants for their arrest. “It makes the victim panic because now they’re seeing themselves on this broadcast, and it’s a screen capture from when they were actually talking with the scammer from their own webcam,” Mason adds. The effect can potentially push the person into sending money or following demands from the scammers.

Telegram did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment on the blackmail scams contained in Yahoo Boy channels. Last year, Telegram 

[removed more than a dozen Yahoo Boy channels](https://archive.ph/o/c037F/https://www.wired.com/story/yahoo-boys-scammers-facebook-telegram-tiktok-youtube/)after WIRED reported on their public activity; however, the scammers still have a presence on the platform and[other social media platforms](https://archive.ph/o/c037F/https://www.wired.com/story/yahoo-boys-scammers-facebook-telegram-tiktok-youtube/), including Facebook, WhatsApp, and YouTube.Messages shared within Telegram channels show how the fraudsters are quick to evolve their cons, use new technologies, and widely share or sell advice with each other. For instance, when people 

[moved to Chinese alternative Rednote](https://archive.ph/o/c037F/https://www.wired.com/story/red-note-tiktok-xiaohongshu/)ahead of the propossed ban TikTok ban in the US earlier this month, Yahoo Boys recommended targeting people who had joined the app.Within one Telegram channel, which has 10,000 subscribers, a scammer explained the steps needed to create false news videos and mocked-up front pages of newspapers over a series of messages. “In blackmailing (BM) work we get two different types which are: TV news [and] newspapers,” the first message says.

In subsequent messages, they gave examples of text that can be inserted into the script for the news bulletin, which says the alleged victim has been “accused of distributing nude images and videos without consent.” All a scammer following the tutorial needs to do is substitute the name and town of their victim and add any pictures they have.

The tutorial suggests headlines for news articles, such as: “Local Man Accused of Online Blackmail and Harassment.” It also lists the names of US TV news networks, cable news, and “specialized news”—it listed 17 news outlets ranging from ABC News and Fox News, to C-Span and Al Jazeera America. One other cybercriminal shared a video of a folder of blackmail scripts and tutorials needed to create fake news items.

In some fabricated news videos, the news anchor appears to be an AI-generated avatar, although it was not possible to determine which software was being used to create the clips. However, tutorials shared on Telegram also show that the grifters are not always using sophisticated technology: Some apps they point to are simple “meme generators.”

Last year, WIRED reported on how 

[Yahoo Boys are adopting deepfake face-swapping technology](https://archive.ph/o/c037F/https://www.wired.com/story/yahoo-boys-real-time-deepfake-scams/)to make video calls with their targets and try to “prove” their false identities are real. However, Maimon also points to one troubling video shared by Yahoo Boy scammers that appears to show a potential victim making a video to apologize for questioning the scammer’s fake identity.Within the video, the woman says, “I am truly sorry that I called you a fake” and asks the scammer to accept their apology. The individual says they hope they get to meet the person they believe they are in love with in the future, before they start removing their clothes to “make up” for the earlier accusation. “I think that what followed that video was them blackmailing her,” Maimon explains, “and of course posting it on the markets they’re on.”

H76Y8SVG.title: Gizmodo used AI to write a Star Wars story. It was filled with errors. - The Washington Post
H76Y8SVG.markdown:
A few hours after James Whitbrook clocked into work at Gizmodo on Wednesday, he received a note from his editor in chief: Within 12 hours, the company would roll out articles written by artificial intelligence. Roughly 10 minutes later, a story by “Gizmodo Bot” posted on the site about the chronological order of Star Wars movies and television shows.

Whitbrook — a deputy editor at Gizmodo who writes and edits articles about science fiction — quickly read the story, which he said he had not asked for or seen before it was published. He catalogued 18 “concerns, corrections and comments” about the story in an email to Gizmodo’s editor in chief, Dan Ackerman, noting the bot put the Star Wars TV series “Star Wars: The Clone Wars” in the wrong order, omitted any mention of television shows such as “Star Wars: Andor” and the 2008 film also entitled “Star Wars: The Clone Wars,” inaccurately formatted movie titles and the story’s headline, had repetitive descriptions, and contained no “explicit disclaimer” that it was written by AI except for the “Gizmodo Bot” byline.

The article quickly prompted an outcry among staffers who complained in the company’s internal Slack messaging system that the error-riddled story [was](https://variety.com/2023/digital/news/io9-ai-generated-star-wars-article-errors-1235662194/) “actively hurting our reputations and credibility,” showed “zero respect” for journalists and should be deleted immediately, according to messages obtained by The Washington Post. The story was written using a combination of Google Bard and ChatGPT, according to a G/O Media staff member familiar with the matter. (G/O Media owns several digital media sites including Gizmodo, Deadspin, The Root, Jezebel and The Onion.)

“I have never had to deal with this basic level of incompetence with any of the colleagues that I have ever worked with,” Whitbrook said in an interview. “If these AI [chatbots] can’t even do something as basic as put a Star Wars movie in order one after the other, I don’t think you can trust it to [report] any kind of accurate information.”

The irony that the turmoil was happening at Gizmodo, a publication dedicated to covering technology, was undeniable. On June 29, Merrill Brown, the editorial director of G/O Media, had cited the organization’s editorial mission as a reason to embrace AI. Because G/O Media owns several sites that cover technology, he wrote, it has a responsibility to “do all we can to develop AI initiatives relatively early in the evolution of the technology."

“These features aren’t replacing work currently being done by writers and editors,” Brown said in announcing to staffers that the company would roll out a trial to test “our editorial and technological thinking about use of AI.” “There will be errors, and they’ll be corrected as swiftly as possible,” he promised.

Gizmodo’s error-plagued test speaks to a larger debate about the role of AI in the news.** **Several reporters and editors said they don’t trust chatbots to create well-reported and thoroughly fact-checked articles. They fear business leaders want to thrust the technology into newsrooms with insufficient caution. When trials go poorly, it ruins employee morale as well as the reputation of the outlet, they argue.

Artificial intelligence experts said many large language models still have technological deficiencies that make them an untrustworthy source for journalism unless humans are deeply involved in the process. Left unchecked, they said, artificially generated news stories could spread disinformation, sow political discord and significantly impact media organizations.

“The danger is to the trustworthiness of the news organization,” said Nick Diakopoulos, an associate professor of communication studies and computer science at Northwestern University. “If you’re going to publish content that is inaccurate, then I think that’s probably going to be a credibility hit to you over time.”

Mark Neschis, a G/O Media spokesman, said the company would be “derelict” if it did not experiment with AI. “We think the AI trial has been successful,” he said in a statement. “In no way do we plan to reduce editorial headcount because of AI activities.” He added: “We are not trying to hide behind anything, we just want to get this right. To do this, we have to accept trial and error.”

In a Slack message reviewed by The Post, Brown told disgruntled employees Thursday that the company is “eager to thoughtfully gather and act on feedback.” “There will be better stories, ideas, data projects and lists that will come forward as we wrestle with the best ways to use the technology,” he said. The note drew 16 thumbs down emoji, 11 wastebasket emoji, six clown emoji, two face palm emoji and two poop emoji, according to screenshots of the Slack conversation.

News media organizations are wrestling with how to use AI chatbots, which can now craft essays, poems and stories often indistinguishable from human-made content. Several media sites that have tried using AI in newsgathering and writing have suffered [high-profile disasters](https://www.washingtonpost.com/media/2023/01/17/cnet-ai-articles-journalism-corrections/). G/O Media seems undeterred.

Earlier this week, Lea Goldman, the deputy editorial director at G/O Media, notified employees on Slack that the company had “commenced limited testing” of AI-generated stories on four of its sites, including A.V. Club, Deadspin, Gizmodo and The Takeout, according to messages The Post viewed. “You may spot errors. You may have issues with tone and/or style,” Goldman wrote. “I am aware you object to this writ large and that your respective unions have already and will continue to weigh in with objections and other issues.”

Employees quickly messaged back with concern and skepticism. “None of our job descriptions include editing or reviewing AI-produced content,” one employee said. “If you wanted an article on the order of the Star Wars movies you … could’ve just asked,” said another. “AI is a solution looking for a problem,” a worker said. “We have talented writers who know what we’re doing. So effectively all you’re doing is wasting everyone’s time.”

Several AI-generated articles were spotted on the company’s sites, including the Star Wars story on Gizmodo’s io9 vertical, which covers topics related to science fiction. On its sports site Deadspin, an AI “Deadspin Bot” wrote a story on the 15 most valuable professional sports franchises with limited valuations of the teams and was corrected on July 6 with no indication of what was wrong. Its food site The Takeout had a “Takeout Bot” byline a story on “the most popular fast food chains in America based on sales” that provided no sales figures. On July 6, Gizmodo appended a correction to its Star Wars story noting that “the episodes’ rankings were incorrect” and had been fixed.

Gizmodo’s union released a statement on Twitter decrying the stories. “This is unethical and unacceptable,” [they wrote](https://twitter.com/gmgunion/status/1676705007201075201). “If you see a byline ending in ‘Bot,’ don’t click it.” Readers who click on the Gizmodo Bot byline itself are told these “stories were produced with the help of an AI engine.”

Diakopoulos, of Northwestern University, said chatbots can produce articles that are of poor quality. The bots, which train on data from places like Wikipedia and Reddit and use that to help them to predict the next word that’s likely to come in a sentence, still have technical issues that make them hard to trust in reporting and writing, he said.

Chatbots are prone to sometimes make up facts, omit information, write language that skews into opinion, regurgitate racial and sexist content, poorly summarize information or completely fabricate quotes, he said.

News companies must have “editing in the loop,” if they are to use bots, he added, but said it can’t rest on one person, and there needs to be multiple reviews of the content to ensure it is accurate and adheres to the media company’s style of writing.

But the dangers are not only to the credibility of media organizations, news researchers said. Sites have also started using AI to create fabricated content, which could turbocharge the dissemination of misinformation and create political chaos.

The media watchdog NewsGuard [said](https://www.newsguardtech.com/special-reports/ai-tracking-center/) that at least 301 AI-generated news sites exist that operate with “no human oversight and publish articles written largely or entirely by bots,” and span 13 languages, including English, Arabic, Chinese and French. They create content that is sometimes false, such as celebrity death hoaxes or entirely fake events, researchers wrote.

Organizations are incentivized to use AI in generating content, NewsGuard analysts said, because ad-tech companies often put digital ads onto sites “without regard to the nature or quality” of the content, creating an economic incentive to use AI bots to churn out as many articles as possible for hosting ads.

Lauren Leffer, a Gizmodo reporter and member of the Writers Guild of America, East union, said this is a “very transparent” effort by G/O Media to get more ad revenue because AI can quickly create articles that generate search and click traffic and cost far less to produce than those by a human reporter.

She added the trial has demoralized reporters and editors who feel their concerns about the company’s AI strategy have gone unheard and are not valued by management. It isn’t that journalists don’t make mistakes on stories, she added, but a reporter has incentive to limit errors because they are held accountable for what they write — which doesn’t apply to chatbots.

Leffer also noted that as of Friday afternoon, the Star Wars story has gotten roughly 12,000 page views on Chartbeat, a tool that tracks news traffic. That pales in comparison to the nearly 300,000 page views a human-written story on NASA has generated in the past 24 hours, she said.

“If you want to run a company whose entire endeavor is to trick people into accidentally clicking on [content], then [AI] might be worth your time,” she said. “But if you want to run a media company, maybe trust your editorial staff to understand what readers want.”

6PPSIGPB.title: Sophie Vermeulen bestaat niet, maar schreef wel 403 artikels voor magazine Elle, blijkt uit onderzoek van VRT NWS | VRT NWS Nieuws [AUTO-TRANSLATED IN ARC]
6PPSIGPB.markdown:
The magazine Elle used various profiles of fake journalists on its website. Research by VRT NWS shows that in April and May, more than half of the online articles were written by fictional characters using AI. Other publications from the parent company 'Ventures Media' are also participating. According to the company, it was a test.

# Sophie Vermeulen does not exist, but she did write 403 articles for Elle magazine, according to research by VRT NWS.

## In short:

- The magazine Elle used fake journalists and AI to 'write' more than half of the online articles in certain months, without making this clear to the readers. 
- Other brands of parent company 'Ventures Media', such as Marie Claire, Forbes, and Psychologies, also made use of fabricated profiles and AI-generated content. 
- Following inquiries from VRT NWS, the names and profiles were adjusted and a disclaimer appeared with the articles: "This content was generated using AI." 

Sophie Vermeulen and Marta Peeters are, at first glance, inspiring women who write online articles for Elle. [Marta](https://archive.ph/eTxo4) is a fashion and lifestyle journalist from Antwerp with a background in communication studies, while [Sophie](https://archive.ph/fVQRU) researches lifestyle and culture and enjoys taking long walks in nature.

We first tracked them down via a tip about articles on Elle's website that seemed strangely written. If we take a closer look at the profiles, we quickly see that something is wrong.

## Sophie Vermeulen has an archive photo

[Sophie's photo](https://this-person-does-not-exist.com/img/avatar-gen064d009d13ef0ae5de5f1c16b1a26260.jpg) appears in the database of the website 'This Person Does Not Exist', a website that uses artificial intelligence to generate faces of people who do not exist. Her email address, as listed on the website, does not exist, and on social media, her photo appears in [profiles](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nina-hanna/) of people all over the world with different names.

Even while working at Elle, she had already undergone a name change. On the 'Wayback Machine' internet archive, we found that in February of this year, the profile with the same photo and biography bore a different name. The alleged journalist with a passion for fashion and beauty was then still called [Justine Terme](https://web.archive.org/web/20250208064950/https://www.elle.be/nl/author/justine) . 

## Marta Peeters has a photo that was taken with AI.

According to 'Sightengine's' AI detector, Marta's photo was also generated by AI with 99 percent certainty. We find no personal email address on her profile, and we cannot find her on social media. She is the author of both [older articles](https://web.archive.org/web/20250417160116/https://www.elle.be/nl/142950-beste-bestemmingen-voor-een-motorvakantie.html)  that previously had ' [ELLEFR](https://web.archive.org/web/20240714114022/https://www.elle.be/nl/142950-beste-bestemmingen-voor-een-motorvakantie.html) ' listed as the author, and newer articles. Yet, according to the 'Wayback Machine', her profile has only existed since early 2025.

## Also fictional profiles at Marie Claire and Forbes

Elle, Marie Claire, and Forbes all belong to the same parent company, 'Ventures Media'. On the Marie Claire website, articles can be read under the name [Claire De Wilde](https://archive.ph/1AM37) . These articles make up slightly less than half of Marie Claire's online articles this year. In her bio, Claire De Wilde discusses how her enriching experiences lead readers to a fulfilling life. At Forbes, an [Elise Van den Berg](https://archive.ph/DJ3BN) is reportedly at work. Profile photos, social media, and existing email addresses are missing. That also seemed a bit strange to our editorial team.

My enriching experiences are reflected in my writing and lead readers to a fulfilled and balanced life.

Claire De Wilde, fictional character

## Profiles removed in the meantime

We had an initial conversation with an employee of Elle and Marie Claire in which we inquired about the authenticity of Marta, Sophie, and Claire. The employee claimed to know nothing about it, but shortly thereafter, the names of the profiles were changed to ' [ELLE Belgium](https://archive.ph/yz9gZ) ', ' [Marieclaire Belgium](https://archive.ph/GCIib) ', and ' [Forbes Belgium](https://archive.ph/4GgVb) '.

The photos and bios were deleted, and a  [disclaimer](https://archive.ph/x43UX#selection-1337.0-1337.101) was  placed behind every article of the fictional profiles stating, “This content was generated using AI and subsequently reviewed and edited by the editorial team.”

## Even a psychologist who doesn't exist?

Through a Google search on the disclaimer, we spotted another profile, namely [Femke](https://archive.ph/OwrXT) from 'Psychologies'. At the end of June, 44 of the 46 online articles for that month appeared under the name 'Femke', without a surname. According to her profile, she is an “editor specializing in psychology and well-being”. In her articles, she writes that she is an “ [experienced psychologist](https://archive.ph/0RNhD#selection-1099.141-1099.159) ” and refers to “ [my practice](https://archive.ph/2NCBE#selection-1071.361-1071.374) ”. Once again, her profile picture and an existing email address were missing. After our initial contact, an AI disclaimer also appeared for this author.

The example of Femke, who presents herself as a psychologist under a journalistic profile and gives advice in that role, is not only misleading but also legally and socially unacceptable.

Carl Defreyne, Chairman of the Committee of Psychologists

Carl Defreyne, chairman of the Psychologists Commission, reacts with dismay and reminds us that "psychologist" is a protected title. "Unfortunately, cases still surface in which people falsely present themselves as psychologists." The Psychologists Commission monitors the ethics of psychologists. The commission's office will contact the publisher of Psychologies and the Flemish Council for Journalism.

## Limited test by the tech team

Eventually, we secured an interview with an executive from 'Ventures Media'. We were asked not to publish the name or exact position of the interviewee.

The person in charge says: “A test is being conducted by the tech team. We are generating articles that are entirely created by AI and have not been editorially reviewed. Aliases have been used within the framework of the test. However, it remains limited and is ** **separate from the editorial team.”

We generate articles that are entirely created by AI and have not been editorially proofread.

Ventures Media

Specifically regarding 'Femke', who is introduced as a psychologist, the supervisor says: "In the context of the test, it concerned an error that has since been corrected."

The [disclaimer](https://archive.ph/hJMIa#selection-1337.0-1337.47) behind the articles was changed again after the interview to “This content was generated using AI”. Whereas the disclaimer previously mentioned a human editorial team that had proofread everything, that team is now no longer named.  

## More than half of Elle's online articles

So the supervisor said that the test was 'limited'. But the articles by the fictional characters Marta and Sophie at Elle are not a fringe phenomenon. We have seen a sharp increase in their writing activity in recent months. More than half of the articles on the Elle website in recent months have been written by the two non-existent journalists.

Sophie Vermeulen, for example, 'wrote' 403 articles since the beginning of this year. Marta Peeters had 150. In the graph below, the green and dark purple parts of the bar show the share of fake journalists on the Elle website.

Most articles appear to be translated from the French-language version of Elle. Those translations also seem to be the work of AI. You notice this, for example, in the fact that [an article about the ultimate wedding destination](https://archive.ph/dcSRf) refers to “Île Maurice”. A Dutch-speaking audience would not expect that. In Dutch, that island is called “Mauritius”. Some  [other articles](https://archive.ph/lQT09)  seem to be inspired by articles from [other magazines](https://archive.ph/uvgwv) in other languages.

Newsrooms must be transparent about the use of AI in news production.

Charlotte Michils, Flemish Association of Journalists

## Are journalists not allowed to use AI then?

According to Charlotte Michils of the Flemish Association of Journalists, the code of ethics is clear: "On the one hand, every journalistic piece must meet high quality standards with an editor-in-chief as the ultimate responsible party; on the other hand, one must be transparent when using AI and maintain control over the content so that it meets the quality requirements."

We understand that the use of aliases can lead to confusion.

Ventures Media

'Ventures Media' announces that it has changed course: "We understand that the use of aliases can lead to confusion, and therefore we have now adjusted that practice to make it clearer in the future and also to indicate that the content was created using AI."

We did not find the fake profiles in the print version of Elle and the other magazines.

4YN84UKT.title: Harper’s Bazaar maakte onjuiste samenvattingen met AI voor artikel over Nederlandse boeken [AUTO-TRANSLATED IN ARC]
4YN84UKT.markdown:
# Harper's Bazaar created incorrect summaries using AI for an article about Dutch books.

Harper's Bazaar used artificial intelligence while writing an article in a manner inconsistent with the magazine's internal guidelines and rules. Editor-in-chief Miluska van 't Lam told Villamedia this after writer Thomas Heerma van Voss concluded that Harper's Bazaar used ChatGPT for an article.

Heerma van Voss wrote in an extensive article about the issue regarding the [Low Countries](https://www.de-lage-landen.com/article/kunstmatige-intelligentie/) .

He was informed that his book 'Het Archief' was mentioned by Harper's Bazaar in an article about 'the five best Dutch books from Harper's Bazaar'. However, it turned out that the summary of his book did not correspond to the actual content.

After reading the summaries of the other books on the list, Heerma van Voss suspected that the editor on duty had used ChatGPT. “I contacted the editors of Harper's Bazaar. I shared my concerns and my strong suspicion that these texts had been written by artificial intelligence. My request: whether this could be taken offline as soon as possible and subsequently rectified. My question: what on earth had happened here?”

He received no explanation, but was informed that the article in question would be taken offline. After several emails, he received a reply stating that errors had been made during the creation of the article and that a new version would be released. It was also stated that this matter would be handled further internally with the editorial team.

**'Downright problematic'**

 
Heerma van Voss calls the incident “extremely reprehensible”.

That someone summarizes books sloppily, that a freelancer cannot read everything completely for such a list: it is all understandable. But strange, no, downright problematic, is when a major fashion magazine feels compelled to publish a top list of books, while no one even takes the trouble to read the back covers of the works in question.

He also refers to [the outrage](https://www.villamedia.nl/artikel/verwijt-dat-feitenchecks-op-facebook-hebben-geleid-tot-censuur-is-onterecht) that arose earlier this week over Mark Zuckerberg's measure to [no longer use fact-checkers at Meta in America](https://www.villamedia.nl/artikel/meta-stopt-met-factcheckers-maar-europese-commissie-neemt-nog-geen-maatregelen) .

Facebook and Instagram will thereby follow in the footsteps of open sewer X: the apps will become a receptacle for the most idiotic and offensive disinformation. In such circumstances, newspapers and magazines play a crucial role. And that role amounts to everything Harper's Bazaar failed to do in this regard.

No accountability. No apology. Hiding behind empty, impersonal language, and where possible accusing the person you call out on a lack of 'respect'. Only making adjustments when caught, and even then quietly. “These are all steps that further erode the truth, a process that is already having terrible consequences worldwide. And so people stumble on and on, heading towards ruin.”

**'Regret'**

 
Following questions about this matter, editor-in-chief Miluska van 't Lam shared the following response a day later.

The use of AI for writing articles is not in accordance with our internal guidelines and rules. We deeply regret the course of events and appropriate measures have been taken. We take our journalistic role seriously and will ensure that this does not happen again in the future.

## Join the conversation

GZPDZKPF.title: Commentary: Did AI really defend the KKK at the end of my column? Let's discuss
GZPDZKPF.markdown:
Journalism schools teach that writers should report the news, not 

*be*the news. But what happens when one of your articles goes viral — not for its content but rather for how an AI doohickey swallowed up what you wrote and upchucked a controversial summation?Welcome to my week.

On Feb. 25, the Times published my 

*columna*about the 100th anniversary of[when Anaheim voters kicked four Ku Klux Klan members off the City Council](https://archive.ph/o/E06AX/https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-02-25/anaheim-ku-klux-klan-council-recall-1925). That many readers seethed at my assertion that the lack of attention paid to the anniversary was unsurprising to me since Anaheim is a place that loves to “celebrate the positive.” More than a few insisted that the KKK in 1920s Orange County wasn’t as bad as in the South, which was such an O.C. response that I didn’t give it a second thought.No, the real fun started Monday, when the The Times launched Insights. It’s an artificial-intelligence-generated tool that reviews the article to affix a ranking on where the piece supposedly lands on the political spectrum. (My Klan piece, for instance? It’s apparently “Left,” which is as surprising a conclusion as the end of the original “Karate Kid.”)

This feature also offers a bullet-point summary, alternative viewpoints and relevant links from across the internet of other news articles, columns and reports. 

Other recent columns of mine got “Center Left,” “Center” and even a “Center Right.” I’m still missing “Right” on my 

*lotería*card.[In a letter to readers](https://archive.ph/o/E06AX/https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-03-03/a-letter-to-readers)introducing the feature, L.A. Times owner Dr. Patrick Soon-Shiong wrote that he believes “providing more varied viewpoints supports our journalistic mission and will help readers navigate the issues facing this nation.”

Well, it didn’t take long for one of Mr. Insights’, well, insights to make people see red. 

Linking to articles critical of the KKK, it said: “Local historical accounts occasionally frame the 1920s Klan as a product of ‘white Protestant culture’ responding to societal changes rather than an explicitly hate-driven movement, 

*minimizing its ideological threat.*”The italics are mine, so put a pin on that phrase because it’s important.

Soon, the headlines started: 

*It only took a day for L.A. Times’ new AI tool to sympathize with the KKK.*

*L.A. Times pulls new AI tool off article after it defends the KKK.*

*The L.A. Times’ new AI tool sympathized with the KKK.*

And on and on it went. Some of the writers of the articles either excised the phrase “minimizing its ideological threat” or seemed to pretend it didn’t exist. But that part of the sentence is crucial: It makes the point that too many people in Orange County have historically minimized the dangers of the KKK.

The AI tool may have been guilty of fuzzy and clumsy phrasing, but it did 

*not*defend or sympathize with the KKK.Journalists like to complain that critics of their articles don’t read past the headline. Well, this was a case of journalists not reading past the first clause of a sentence.

In fact, as I pointed out on X, that citation was correct. I was actually shocked AI got such a crucial point right. But I was also annoyed that the two other bullet points — including one that linked to one of 

[my columns in 2018](https://archive.ph/o/E06AX/https://capitalandmain.com/orange-county-parents-change-name-school-honors-klan-member-0219)about the Klan in O.C. — were wildly out of context, but no one else seemed to care.Either way, friends began texting me stories from local and national outlets within hours of my column’s appearing online claiming the AI tool used by the Times outright endorsed the KKK. Some readers announced they were canceling their Times subscriptions, saying they didn’t want their money to support a publication that, somehow, gave a thumbs-up to the Klan.

Insights’ rambling, overly long deconstruction of my 

*columna*caused some people to conclude it was downplaying the KKK’s awfulness.But to proclaim it literally endorsed the hate group?

Only one reporter reached out to me as the writer of the column that provoked AI Klan-gate. My opinion would have been given gladly and AI-free to all comers. 

As a journalist, I’d hope that my contemporaries who reported on the situation would have been a little more precise about describing the language they saw on the feature. The net effect was to make it seem like the AI tool had practically burned a cross to show its support for the KKK on a column that explicitly denounced the Invisible Empire.

They were more hung up on The Times’ AI tool and not the actual journalism that preceded it, which makes me think they didn’t even read my column. Thanks, pals!

As for the readers who said that canceling their Times subscriptions was a way to lodge their anger at The Times for using Insights, here’s the thing: You have to press a button to trigger the thing. Like the comments section, you can engage with it or not. You can choose just to read what the humans have to say — and criticize or laud them. Why, if you ignore the AI 

*pendejada*enough, it could very well pick up its digital football and go home.If there’s a silver lining to any of this, it’s that I may be a prophet. In December, 

[I predicted](https://archive.ph/o/E06AX/https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2024-12-27/california-predictions-for-2025)that whatever AI program the Los Angeles Times would end up using on its opinion pieces, it would self-immolate the moment it encountered one of mine.That should count as a 

*lotería*square, right?

PM3WEYZZ.title: The LA Times Has 'Moved On' From AI-Driven Bias Meter After KKK Snafu
PM3WEYZZ.markdown:
*Editor’s Note: This story has been updated to clarify the difference between the Los Angeles Times’ “bias meter,” which was never launched, and its AI-generated Insights feature, which provides context on some editorial articles. *

The Los Angeles Times has “moved on” from the AI-generated “bias meter” that owner Patrick Soon-Shiong wanted to establish, managing editor Hector Becerra said in a recent meeting.

There paper is, however, still using the Insights feature, which is also AI-generated. Insights, which functions somewhat like Grok or Community Notes on X, made headlines last month when the note it added to Gustavo Arellano’s column about the KKK, included the phrase that the Klan was not “an explicitly hate-driven movement.”

In an [April 4 Zoom meeting](https://ofsla.com/), shared to a blog for former Times staffers, Becerra said he was relieved that an actual meter — like those displayed on [All Sides](https://www.allsides.com/media-bias/media-bias-rating-methods) — never came to pass. “Thank God there is no real bias meter … I can’t say that anybody was a huge fan of it. It’s a bit of a distraction, but I think people mostly moved on.”

The following day, the Insights note was yanked from that column but is still in use on other editorials. It is not used on any news stories.

Becerra explained in the April 4 meeting, “That citation did not defend the KKK. But it was written in such a passive kind of voice and almost, like, backwards, that I think some people misread it as almost being too soft. And then it got picked up by media: ‘AI defends KKK.’”

He added, “I have to be honest with you, that kind of pissed me off, because media, in general, we should be better than that. There is so much disinformation going on. Let’s be precise about what it actually said and what it actually did.”

As Arellano himself pointed out in a follow-up to his column on March 7, only part of what the AI had added was included in the news pick-ups.

“Local historical accounts occasionally frame the 1920s Klan as a product of ‘white Protestant culture’ responding to societal changes rather than an explicitly hate-driven movement, *minimizing its ideological threat*,” Arellano wrote, italicizing the last four words. 

Arellano noted at the end of his March 7 article that he had earlier [predicted](https://web.archive.org/web/20250307114431/https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2024-12-27/california-predictions-for-2025) that “whatever AI program the Los Angeles Times would end up using on its opinion pieces, it would self-immolate the moment it encountered one of mine.”

On March 3 when he introduced Insights, Soon-Shiong said that it would “offer readers an instantly accessible way to see a wide range of different AI-enabled perspectives alongside the positions presented in the article.” He also said, “I believe providing more varied viewpoints supports our journalistic mission and will help readers navigate the issues facing this nation.”

Z7DR3YI3.title: Google is experimentally replacing news headlines with AI clickbait nonsense
Z7DR3YI3.markdown:
Did you know that *BG3 *players exploit children**Qi2 slows older Pixels**? If we wrote those misleading headlines, readers would rip us a new one — but Google is experimentally beginning to replace the original headlines on stories it serves with AI nonsense like that. (*Update: **this is no longer an experiment*

I read a lot of my bedtime news via Google Discover, aka “swipe right on your Samsung Galaxy or Google Pixel homescreen until you see a news feed appear,” and that’s where these new AI headlines are beginning to show up.

They’re not all bad. For example, “**Origami model wins prize**” and “**Hyundai, Kia gain share**” seem fine, even if not remotely as interesting as the original headlines. (“[Hyundai and Kia are lapping the competition as US market share reaches a new record](https://electrek.co/2025/12/01/hyundai-kia-race-past-rivals-set-record-us-market-share/)” and “[14-year-old wins prize for origami that can hold 10,000 times its own weight](https://www.sciencealert.com/14-year-old-wins-prize-for-origami-that-can-hold-10000-times-its-own-weight)” sound like they’re actually worth a click!)

But in the seeming attempt to boil down every story to four words or less, Google’s new headline experiment is attaching *plenty* of misleading and inane headlines to journalists’ work, and with little disclosure that Google’s AI is rewriting them.

The very first one I saw was “**Steam Machine price revealed**,” which it most certainly was not! Valve won’t reveal that till next year. *Ars Technica*’s original headline

**“Microsoft developers using AI**”? No shit, Sherlock. (That one was tacked on my colleague Tom Warren’s story about “*How* Microsoft’s developers are using AI

*Reached for comment, my colleague Tom Warren said: “lol wtf Google.”*

I also saw Google try to claim that “**AMD GPU tops Nvidia**,” as if AMD had announced a new groundbreaking graphics card, when [the actual ](https://wccftech.com/radeon-rx-9070-xt-outsells-the-entire-nvidia-rtx-50-series-on-popular-german-retailer/)*Wccftech* story is about how a single German retailer managed to sell more AMD units than Nvidia units within a single week’s span. *Wccftech*’s headline was relatively responsible, but Google turned it into clickbait.

Then there are the headlines that simply don’t make sense out of context, something real human editors avoid like plague. What does “**Schedule 1 farming backup**” mean? How about “**AI tag debate heats**”?

Make no mistake, the problem isn’t just that these AI headlines are bad. It’s that Google is taking away our agency to market our own work, like if we’d written a book and the bookstore decided to replace its cover.

We try hard to craft headlines that invite readers in, ones that responsibly encapsulate the news, ones that help you understand *why* a story matters right away and get you excited when it’s justified. (Does my headline for this story seem the right amount of excited?) And yet Google seems to think it can just replace these headlines, in a way that might confuse our readers and think *we’re* the ones generating clickbait, since our publications’ names appear right next to them.

Google does disclose that *something* about these news items is “Generated with AI, which can make mistakes,” but not what, and readers only see that message if they tap the “See more” button:

*What Google shows me when I tap “see more*.”

It’s too easy for readers to think we intentionally send our stories to Google Discover with these headlines.

The good news is, this is a Google experiment. If there’s enough backlash, the company probably won’t proceed. “These screenshots show a small UI experiment for a subset of Discover users,” Google spokesperson Mallory Deleon tells *The Verge*. “We are testing a new design that changes the placement of existing headlines to make topic details easier to digest before they explore links from across the web.”

But the overall trend at Google has been to prioritize its own products at the expense of sending clicks to news websites. While the company [swears it isn’t destroying the web with AI search](https://www.theverge.com/news/720069/google-ai-overviews-search-web-traffic-stable), you’d be hard-pressed to find a news outlet that agrees, and even [Google has admitted in court](https://www.theverge.com/news/773928/google-open-web-rapid-decline) that “the open web is already in rapid decline.”

It’s the reason *The Verge* now has a subscription[Google Zero](https://www.theverge.com/24167865/google-zero-search-crash-housefresh-ai-overviews-traffic-data-audience) without your help.

*Update, December 4th: **A day or so after this story, Google seems to have changed its AI experiment and *[I’m seeing headlines return, but the AI is still a bit confused](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/838354/googles-ai-news-bot-is-still-confused-but-no-longer-replacing-our-headlines).

[42 Comments](#comments)**Follow topics and authors** from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

PXKLCK9L.title: Google won’t stop replacing our news headlines with terrible AI
PXKLCK9L.markdown:
In early December, [I brought you the news](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/835839/google-discover-ai-headlines-clickbait-nonsense) that Google has begun replacing *Verge* headlines, and those of our competitors, with AI clickbait nonsense in its content feed. Google [appeared to be backing away from the experiment](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/838354/googles-ai-news-bot-is-still-confused-but-no-longer-replacing-our-headlines), but now tells *The Verge* that its AI headlines in Google Discover are a feature, one that “performs well for user satisfaction.” I once again see lots of misleading claims every time I check my phone.

# Google won’t stop replacing our news headlines with terrible AI

It now says AI headlines are a ‘feature,’ not an experiment.

It now says AI headlines are a ‘feature,’ not an experiment.

Like I explained last month, these AI headlines are akin to a bookstore replacing the covers of the books it puts on display — only here, the “bookstore” is the news tab that appears when you swipe right on the homescreen of a Samsung Galaxy or Google Pixel phone, and the “cover” might be a AI-generated lie instead of the truth.

## Add Verge on Google

Add Verge as a preferred source to see more of our reporting on Google.

[Add us on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=theverge.com)

For example, Google’s AI claimed last week that **“US reverses foreign drone ban,”** citing and linking to [this  PCMag story](https://www.pcmag.com/news/dji-and-the-us-drone-ban-explained-our-expert-answers-every-question?test_uuid=04IpBmWGZleS0I0J3epvMrC&test_variant=B) for the news. That’s not just false — 

*PCMag*took pains to explain that it’s false

*in the story that Google links to!*

From *PCMag*’s story, bolding theirs:


I saw a headline saying that the drone ban was dropped. Is that true?No. While it’s true the Commerce Departmentended its effortsto restrict DJI and other drones from import in Jan. 2026, it only did so because it would be redundant in the wake of the FCC actions. The Commerce Department is a separate entity from the FCC, and its proposed restrictions were never put in place to begin with. Some reports on the Commerce Department’s decision have misleading headlines that could make you think the government did an about-face, so I don’t blame you for being confused.

What does the author of that *PCMag *story think? “It makes me feel icky,” Jim Fisher tells me over the phone. “I’d encourage people to click on stories and read them, and not trust what Google is spoon-feeding them.”

He says Google should be using the headline that humans wrote, and if Google needs a summary, it can use the ones that publications already submit to help search engines parse our work.

Google claims it’s not rewriting headlines. It characterizes these new offerings as “trending topics,” even though each “trending topic” presents itself as one of our stories, links to our stories, and uses our images, all without competent fact-checking to ensure the AI is getting them right.

In some ways, Google’s current implementation isn’t quite as bad as it was a month ago. I’ve seen fewer examples of egregious clickbait, partly because Google Discover is now serving me quite a few unadulterated news stories alongside its AI ones — though it does cut off their genuine headlines far too quickly, making many tough to read.

The AI is also no longer restricted to roughly four words per headline, so I no longer see nonsense headlines like “Microsoft developers using AI” or “AI tag debate heats.” (Instead, I occasionally see tripe like “**Fares: Need AAA & AA Games**” or “**Dispatch sold millions; few avoided romance**.”)

But Google’s AI has no clue what parts of these stories are new, relevant, significant, or true, and it can easily confuse one story for another.

On December 26th, Google told me that “**Steam Machine price & HDMI details emerge**.” They hadn’t. On January 11th, Google proclaimed that “**ASUS ROG Ally X arrives**.” (It arrived [in 2024](https://www.theverge.com/24204770/asus-rog-ally-x-review-handheld-gaming-pc); the new Xbox Ally [arrived months ago](https://www.theverge.com/games/799698/xbox-ally-x-review-asus-microsoft-full-screen-experience).) On January 20th, it wrote that “**Glasses-free 3D tech wows**,” introducing readers to “New 3D tech called Immensity from Leia” — but linking to [this  TechRadar story](https://www.techradar.com/televisions/i-saw-2-next-gen-3d-tvs-without-glasses-that-use-a-new-tech-that-changes-everything-heres-how-it-works) about an entirely different company called Visual Semiconductor. I found another that claimed to be about a GPU maker commenting 

[on the RAM shortage](https://www.theverge.com/report/839506/ram-shortage-price-increases-pc-gaming-smartphones); it linked instead to

[a](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20251212VL206/sk-hynix-dram-competition-manufacturing-cxmt.html)about a RAM maker.

*Digitimes*storyI’m particularly frustrated when I see bait-and-switch headlines on *Verge* stories, of course, and worried they’re taking away our ability to market our own work.

Google boiled down my colleague Jay Peters’ story about how RGB stripe OLED monitors can [unlock sharper text and more accurate colors](https://www.theverge.com/tech/855247/asus-oled-gaming-monitors-rgb-stripe-ces-2026) to the boring “**New OLED Gaming Monitors Debut**.” My story about letting you [experience an immersive 3D demo of the Lego Smart Brick like you’re there with us at CES](https://www.theverge.com/tech/861322/lego-smart-brick-vr-180-3d-video-demo-ces-2026) became “**Lego Smart Play launches March 1**,” a date that wasn’t news by the time Google wrote that! And Google AI decided to advertise our [big Verge Awards at CES 2026](https://www.theverge.com/tech/858494/ces-2026-best-new-tech-tv-car-wearable) story as “**Robots & AI Take CES**,” which was basically the opposite of our conclusion in that story.

And yet, our new AI overlords are not effectively weeding out the worst *human* clickbait in exchange for our fealty. One headline that Google’s AI didn’t overwrite was “**Star Wars Outlaws Free Download Available For Less Than 24 Hours**” by *Screen Rant*. Here’s what the author of that story reveals halfway down the post:

Just the one code being given away when thousands of people are likely to get involved feels a bit stingy, although at the time of writing Ubisoft’s post hasn’t exactly blown up, so you might be in with a shot.


Yes, Ubisoft gave away *a single copy of a game* on X, in a giveaway only open to residents of the UK, yet Google’s news bot decided that *Screen Rant*’s FOMO clickbait was fine to serve up without tweaks at all.

Here’s the statement from Google spokesperson Jennifer Kutz about the Google feature:

We launched a new

[feature](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/ai-features-web-content/)last year in Discover to help people explore topics that are covered by multiple creators and websites. The feature includes a helpful AI-powered overview of the topic, a featured image, and links to related stories. The overview headline reflects information across a range of sites, and is not a rewrite of an individual article headline. This feature performs well for user satisfaction, and we continue to experiment with the UI to help people click through and explore content on the web.

Google declined our request for an interview to more fully explain the idea.

I don’t know how broadly Google is showing these “trending topics” AI headlines yet, but it seems the company is testing them beyond the Google Discover news feed, too. I’ve recently seen some of them appear as push notifications to my phone; tapping them takes me to a Google Gemini chatbot that attempts to summarize a recent piece of news.

*Disclosure: Vox Media, *The Verge*’s parent company, has  filed a lawsuit against Google, seeking damages from its illegal ad tech monopoly.*

A97FL2RY.title: Berechtigte Kritik an «KI-Sündern» oder «Hexenjagd»? Wie die KI durch die Medien fegt [AUTO-TRANSLATED IN ARC]
A97FL2RY.markdown:
##   Those Artificial intelligence in journalism   "The machine wrote that!" – How AI is sweeping through the media

  Journalistic writing is increasingly merging with automatically generated text. At the same time, the media are exposing "AI writers" amidst great uproar. Are limits necessary? 

  **Shortly:**

- Journalists and politicians worldwide are being accused of having texts written by AI.
- AI recognition tools like Pangram are becoming increasingly popular, but are considered unreliable and face criticism from experts.
- Media companies can currently be divided into two camps: those who want to prevent AI content in texts, and those who encourage it.
- «Blick» editor-in-chief Rolf Cavalli uses an «AI proofreader» to revise his texts.

On April 10, 2026, Rolf Cavalli published a 

 [commentary.](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.blick.ch/politik/opfer-schuldige-behoerden-warum-die-zeit-davonlaeuft-100-tage-crans-montana-5-bittere-wahrheiten-id21856036.html)One hundred days after the Crans-Montana disaster, the editor-in-chief of "Blick" lists five "bitter truths" he has observed in the way the catastrophe has been handled.Two months later, freelance journalist Esther Diener-Morscher published an 

 [article on «Infosperber».](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.infosperber.ch/medien/die-ki-richtlinien-der-medien-sind-ein-witz/)about Cavalli's analysis. And accuses the "Blick" editor-in-chief of having relied too heavily on AI programs for help in writing.Diener-Morscher praises the "movement" in the text. At the same time, she finds it all sounds too polished. For example: "The victims have faces. The perpetrators only have functions." Sounds good, the journalist thinks – but: What is Cavalli actually trying to say?

 Diener-Morscher also expresses fundamental criticism: the AI guidelines of Swiss media are too liberal, and there is too little transparency regarding the use of AI. She ultimately leaves open the question of whether she believes Cavalli had the text written by a machine. The "Blick" media office is quoted as saying that the editor-in-chief writes his texts "independently."

 Diener-Morscher, however, hints at what she thinks about the text: "Perfect, precise, to the point: as if written by an artificial intelligence."

 Rolf Cavalli, an "AI sinner"?

 It's not that simple. For one thing, there's no consensus on what constitutes a "sin".

 **The debate surrounding artificial intelligence is heating up.**

It is no coincidence that Diener-Morscher's critique appears in the summer of 2026. The industry is at a crucial juncture. Three and a half years after the launch 

 [of Chat-GPT, AI tools have matured to the point](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.tagesanzeiger.ch/chat-gpt-wie-schweizer-mit-ai-sprechen-246901293499)where they are becoming commonplace. Journalists are letting AI conduct research, create headlines, proofread texts, and generate graphics. Humans and machines are beginning to merge.At the same time, every media company is embroiled in a heated debate about how much AI should intervene in the journalistic thought and work process.

 In Germany, former "Tagesspiegel" editor-in-chief 

 [Stephan-Andreas Casdorff caused an uproar in mid-June](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.tagesanzeiger.ch/ki-in-medien-journalist-suspendiert-politiker-unter-druck-169093642770)– along the lines of: "This was written by a machine!" It turns out that Casdorff had indeed had several commentaries written by a machine. The newspaper[stopped publishing them.](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.tagesspiegel.de/in-eigener-sache-editor-at-large-muss-publizistische-aufgaben-vorerst-ruhen-lassen-15708436.html)the collaboration with him. Editor-in-Chief Christian Tretbar[says](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.deutschlandfunk.de/tagesspiegel-chefredakteur-der-mensch-dessen-name-ueber-einem-artikel-steht-muss-auch-wirklich-in-de-100.html)“That’s something we at the ‘Tagesspiegel’ don’t want.” Casdorff himself apologizes for his “huge mistake”.Such cases will erupt around the globe in the first half of 2026: In March, 

 [it will end](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/mar/31/the-new-york-times-drops-freelance-journalist-who-used-ai-to-write-book-review)The New York Times reported on its collaboration with a freelance writer who wrote a book review using AI. And at the end of June,[Cicero magazine also discussed the issue.](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.cicero.de/kultur/schweizer-traditionsmedium-ein-begrundeter-verdacht-und-viele-ungereimtheiten-die-neue-zurcher-zeitung-erlebt-ihren-ki-skandal)The NZZ Germany newspaper has accused the editor-in-chief of writing extensive commentaries using AI. Using the AI detection software Pangram, the magazine concludes that significant portions of Florian Eder's 52 articles were AI-generated. The accusations are based on a[blog post.](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://plagiatsgutachten.com/blog/ki-stilelemente-nzz-eder/)a controversial plagiarism hunter. The NZZ counters that the program "cannot reliably determine whether a text was written by a human or an artificial intelligence." Eder remains in office.## Politicians are also accused of using artificial intelligence.

At the same time, politicians are accused of having written guest articles or speeches using AI. The platform "Frag Den Staat" 

 [identifies](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://fragdenstaat.de/artikel/exklusiv/2026/06/ich-trete-in-das-vermachtnis-eines-anspruchs/)In early June, speeches and texts by Thuringian Minister-President Mario Voigt were found to have been generated using AI software.[As a result, the renowned Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) removed a guest article by Voigt from its website.](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.faz.net/aktuell/feuilleton/medien-und-film/medienpolitik/zum-ki-verdacht-bei-gastbeitrag-von-mario-voigt-200917046.html).This infuriates the combative Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner so much that he commissions the AI to write a rebuttal: "Write a commentary that brilliantly refutes the (...) text." Döpfner then 

 [publishes the result in "Die Welt."](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.welt.de/debatte/article6a2aad4c6bb5c7fe2e1c1e2a/ki-debatte-um-mario-voigt-die-maschinen-stuermer-von-der-faz-willkommen-im-jahr-2026.html)He immediately adds the prompt, that is, the instruction to the machine. Which in turn[earns him the smug criticism from the FAZ (Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung).](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.faz.net/aktuell/feuilleton/debatten/zukunft-des-journalismus-mathias-doepfner-laesst-ki-fuer-sich-denken-200925012.html)He apparently "had not gotten any further with natural intelligence".And so it goes back and forth.

 The questions being discussed are fundamental in nature: Where does the core of journalistic work lie in the age of AI? And what does the public actually want?

 **The editor-in-chief of "Blick" says he writes himself**

When asked, Rolf Cavalli said: “I write my own commentaries. The insinuation that my commentaries are partly dictated by AI is baseless.” The editor-in-chief of Blick confirmed, however, that he uses AI “for editing and critical feedback.” He stated that he created a prompt for this purpose. The machine then measures his draft commentaries against his own standards, points out weaknesses, and makes suggestions for improvement. “This doesn’t replace a colleague as a proofreader – but it does make my work better.”

 Mirko Lange foresaw conflicts like the Cavalli case. The German lawyer built a software company and worked as a communications consultant. He recently founded a 

 [tech start-up.](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://democracy-intelligence.de/)He founded an institute that focuses on the quality of democratic debate. He stands out for his analyses of AI, journalism, and politics.Lange warns on the phone and in a 

 [LinkedIn essay](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/der-beginn-einer-hexenjagd-auf-ki-texte-mirko-lange-mmexe/)He warns of an AI "witch hunt" and criticizes the use of AI detection tools like Pangram.The entrepreneur says the program is now good at recognizing machine-generated text patterns. But: "The machine compares the linguistic surface of a text with what it has learned as 'typical AI.' '100 percent AI' means: This text closely resembles what language models output. Nothing more."

 It's possible, therefore, that someone uses a writing style that happens to resemble standard AI text. Or: Someone used AI to polish a text, but the underlying ideas came from the author. This isn't a new problem, says Lange: Politicians and journalists have always relied on consultants or proofreaders.

 At the same time, Lange says: AI is the future. "To forgo it would be about as smart as operating a steam engine when everyone else has long since switched to electricity."

 Media professionals, as language workers, are ideally suited to transforming raw AI material into a smart, authentic product. He sees AI as a technological tool that makes users more versatile and faster. But the responsibility for these capabilities always lies with humans.

 For Lange, the crucial boundary is not between humans and machines, but between "sense" and "slop," that is, between "meaning" and "nonsense." Even in the past, people would have spouted plenty of nonsense without AI assistance, and today machines produce accurate information in many situations.

 However, the machine must be used with full awareness of its weaknesses. And according to Lange, that means work. For example, to prevent a text from being "botched" by AI. He sees a great danger here. Anyone who isn't careful relinquishes their own judgment because it's so easy to let the AI argue for them. "The machine sets its own priorities and weights things. Anyone who lets AI take away their judgment, stance, and responsibility is giving up precisely what matters."

 **The editor-in-chief of "Blick" will switch on the machine in spring 2025.**

After many years at CH-Media, Rolf Cavalli has been editor-in-chief of "Blick" since April 2025. He has worked for the Ringier media group since March 2024, and by the beginning of July 2026, he had written 71 opinion pieces. What influence did AI, acting as a "proofreader," have on his commentary?

 With Mirko Lange's warning in mind, we first checked his texts with Pangram to look for patterns. And we read and analyzed the opinions.

 Pangram detects 39 Cavalli texts as being partially or heavily written or supported by AI. The program classifies 32 texts as "100 percent human-written".

 The individual figures are not very reliable. However, the temporal pattern is striking: The program classifies all texts from 2024 up to and including January 2025 as "100 percent human." On April 26, 2025, the first text appears that the tool identifies as having a strong AI component. According to Pangram, AI is then present in Cavalli's texts at irregular intervals – sometimes more, sometimes less.

 It seems as if Cavalli switched on the machine in the spring of 2025.

 The editor-in-chief distrusts Pangram. He writes in response to an inquiry that the program incorrectly classifies rhythmic and dense phrasing as typical of AI. However, he confirms that his AI prompt has been in use since spring 2025.

 When asked, he shared the prompt with this editorial team. It contained eleven content requirements for his text and thirteen questions, which the chat-based GPT (General Performance Task) was supposed to use to check the text for dramaturgy, word choice, style, and rhythm. Cavalli then adopted some of the suggestions from the "AI proofreader," while discarding others.

 The machine's influence is evident in language, as a reading of his texts reveals. For example, the use of certain rhetorical devices increases significantly from spring 2025 onwards. 

 [Studies](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.267.pdf)This shows that there are linguistic devices that AI language models frequently employ. One example is "not A, but B" arguments. Another example is three-part enumerations, often referred to as triads. However, such constructions are also popular among human authors – which is one of the reasons why the models often reproduce them.## Rolf Cavalli and his «Sound»

A 

 [Cavalli commentary](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.blick.ch/politik/skandal-in-der-herzchirurgie-zuerich-teufel-in-weiss-warum-sie-keiner-stoppen-will-id21934139.html)The Maisano case at the University Hospital Zurich from May 2026, for example, stands out with four "not A, but B" figures:*"The patient is*


*no**longer a person,*


*but**a case."*

*"The question is*


*not**just: How could this happen?*


*But**: Why didn't anyone stop it?"*

*"*


*Not that**nobody was paying attention,*


*but**those who were paying attention were not taken seriously for years."*

*"The real power lies*


*not**in the boardroom,*


*but**at the operating table."*

Equally striking: The commentary is full of triads, seven in total, ranging from "Own networks. Own rules. Own loyalties" to "Fame, money, vanity".

 Cavalli replies: "I have been using staccato, triads and similar stylistic devices for years."

 That's correct. He had used lists of three items before. However, from spring 2024 to spring 2025, with one exception, none of his commentaries contain more than two examples. After that, over a dozen texts with six or more triads appear.

 This may have been Cavalli's own decision. According to his own statements, he wanted to deliberately change his style in his new role as editor-in-chief of "Blick" in the spring of 2025, becoming more pointed and accessible. He succeeded: his most recent texts bear witness to a specific "Cavalli sound".

 Perhaps it was the "AI proofreader" that made the corresponding suggestions. Perhaps it was a combination of both. Ultimately, only the author himself can say exactly how many factors were involved.

 One thing is clear: Rolf Cavalli is an early example of how man and machine are growing together.

 What does the editor-in-chief himself think? He sees AI development as an opportunity, he says. But writing weekly commentaries is a process for him. He wrestles with thoughts, theses, and formulations. "When it comes to opinion pieces, my journalistic understanding is clear: writing style shouldn't be delegated, and certainly not one's stance."

 **"The rules of journalism need to be renegotiated."**

What happens when journalism begins to change in such a fundamental way? Felix Simon researches these kinds of questions. The communications scholar works at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism at Oxford University. He regularly publishes on AI in journalism.

 “The journalistic rules were quite clear for a long time,” says Simon. “Now they need to be renegotiated. This is accompanied by strong emotions.”

 In text-based journalism, media outlets worldwide can be roughly divided into two camps. One views AI strictly as a supporting tool and draws a line when it comes to writing journalistic texts. The New York Times, for example, maintains this position in its 

 [guidelines.](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/07/reader-center/how-new-york-times-uses-ai-journalism.html)Fest: "We do not use AI to write our articles." The Financial Times[states:](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.ft.com/content/18337836-7c5f-42bd-a57a-24cdbd06ec51)"Our journalism will continue to be researched, written, and edited by people who are among the best in their fields."On the other side are media companies that advocate a proactive approach to AI. The most prominent proponent is Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner. For him, the "principle of responsibility" applies, as he 

 [explained on his own "Welt" channel.](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9i2FQ-4E3kY)Each author is responsible for the texts published under their own name. How these texts are created is secondary – as long as they are accurate. The only exception: If a text is 100% AI-generated, this must be declared.AI is a neutral technology, argues Döpfner, adding that this was also true for nuclear fission and the internet. "We must be very careful that, unlike illegal drug use, the identity of AI users is not revealed."

 ## Blick CEO: "A powerful commentary originates in the mind of the author"

Döpfner's approach to responsibility is similarly advocated by other media companies, for example by Ringier CEO Marc Walder. Ringier's guidelines permit the extensive use of AI – Cavalli's "AI Checker" is not only allowed, but encouraged.

 “The disruption caused by artificial intelligence is real,” Walder writes in response to an inquiry. “Those who master AI win. Those who don’t, lose.” AI supports journalists in refining their arguments. This also applies to opinion journalism: “At its core, it’s about stance, contextualization, and intellect.”

 But Walder draws a line when it comes to opinions. "A strong commentary always originates in the author's mind," he writes. "The cognitive input, the thesis, and the final judgment must come from a human being." Prompting a commentary? That goes too far for AI enthusiast Walder.

 Tamedia, the media company to which this newsroom belongs, also operates according to the principle of accountability. "We don't see AI as a threat to journalism, but rather consciously focus on an open and proactive approach in all our newsrooms," says editorial director Simon Bärtschi. AI is a very useful tool that can strengthen journalism – provided that responsibility for form and content always remains with the editors.

 Bärtschi also considers commentaries and editorials to be particularly sensitive. "Opinion journalism is an art form. The bar is set higher for me here," he says. "What makes a commentary thrive? Personal stance, personal experience – something a machine can hardly provide."

  **Artificial intelligence is causing fears of losing status.**

How far should we go with AI? Felix Simon advocates a middle ground. He accuses extreme AI skeptics of sometimes overemphasizing the act of journalistic writing. "Talent writers, in particular, are driven by a fear of losing status." Conversely, AI enthusiasts neglect the widespread skepticism among the public regarding AI-generated journalism.

 Last year, Simon commissioned the Reuters Institute to 

 [survey 12,000 people in six countries about their attitudes towards AI-generated news.](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/generative-ai-and-news-report-2025-how-people-think-about-ais-role-journalism-and-society)The result: Only 12 percent feel comfortable with information that is 100 percent AI-generated. If "some human oversight" is involved, that figure rises to 21 percent. If AI only provides support, it's 43 percent. And for news generated exclusively by humans, it's 62 percent.However, it strongly depends on the type of text, says Simon. Automating a weather report is far less controversial than a personal news story. Therefore, it's no coincidence that the current debate has focused on opinions. "Here, we're most interested in the author's thought process. We want to know: What does she think?" Opinions are therefore poorly suited to automation from the audience's perspective. "I advise using AI very cautiously here, and disclosing its use."

 The merging of AI and journalism will continue, the researcher believes. The next generations are growing up with chatbots and similar technologies. "We're already seeing more and more people getting their news from chatbots." Society will therefore increasingly accept AI-supported journalism, even if it isn't enthusiastic about it. "I think it's good that this debate is taking place," says Simon. "Even if emotions are running high right now, we can only rediscover ourselves if we talk about it."

   The morning

 The perfect start to the day with news and stories from Switzerland and the world.     **Mario Stäuble**is the head of the politics and business section. Previously, he was co-editor-in-chief of the Tages-Anzeiger. The lawyer joined the Tages-Anzeiger as a trainee in 2011.

[More information](https://archive.ph/o/Kt6FH/https://www.tagesanzeiger.ch/author/81924614/mario-stauble)
