6P72YK3E.title: De robotjournalist moet geen bullshitgenerator worden
6P72YK3E.markdown:
# The robot journalist must not become a bullshit generator.

 +  Reading list  

 Artificial intelligence: Dutch media are experimenting extensively with 'robot journalism', the simpler sibling of AI. However, this is far from always yielding the desired results. "Then 342 articles had to be taken offline all at once." 

It came as a shock to fans of the local FC. Hundreds of amateur football clubs were assigned an incorrect points total this summer in match reports on the websites of regional newspapers such as 

*De Gelderlander*,*De Stentor*, and*Tubantia*. The cause: not a massive off-day for sports editors, but a glitch in the computer program that writes the reports.Publisher DPG Media launched the 'robot journalism' project this spring. The editorial staff of the 

*Algemeen Dagblad*(AD), with which the regional newspapers collaborate, collects data broken down by municipality regarding sports, weather, or demographic trends. The computer combines this with a template written by an editor and delivers a ready-made article for each municipality. For instance, under the standard headline 'This is how the first teams from [place name] played this weekend', it lists who scored and what the new point total is.So, the latter turned out to be incorrect at the end of May, due to errors in the data originating from the KNVB. "Clubs started calling us, saying: we don't have six points at all, but nine," explains Joris Gerritsen, editor-in-chief of 

*De Gelderlander*and a member of a DPG working group on robot journalism. The error ran throughout the entire dataset. "Then 342 articles had to be taken offline all at once."     

**Read also**News media warn: ChatGPT can undermine journalism's business model

As in other sectors, there is much discussion in journalism about artificial intelligence (AI), particularly 'generative' AI. The popular program ChatGPT from market leader OpenAI produces eerily good texts, and there is open speculation about what this could mean for print journalism.

Maar hoewel individuele journalisten regelmatig experimenteren met ChatGPT – zie inzet – houden grote nieuwsmedia de boot af. Ze richten hun pijlen op het simpele broertje van AI: robotjournalistiek. Wanneer iets precies AI is, is onderwerp van discussie, maar Gerritsen zegt over het DPG-project: „Er zit geen zelflerend mechanisme achter, wat kenmerkend is voor AI. Wij spreken daarom van robotjournalistiek.”

## Oranje auto’s

Het ANP 

[experimenteerde](https://archive.ph/o/rIU4j/https://www.svdj.nl/nieuws/robotjournalistiek-bij-anp-maakt-verslaggever-nog-niet-overbodig/)al in 2017 met robotjournalistiek,*Het Financieele Dagblad*[in 2018](https://archive.ph/o/rIU4j/https://www.svdj.nl/nieuws/waar-blijft-robotjournalistiek-nederland/). Beide proeven stierven een stille dood. DPG kondigde al in 2017 robotberichten op regioniveau aan. Waarom was de tijd nu pas rijp? „Pas sinds vorig jaar heeft elke gemeente een eigen pagina op AD.nl. Dat moesten we eerst regelen”, zegt adjunct-hoofdredacteur van*AD*Regio Mark Langeslag.Zo kan wie in Nunspeet woont, voor lokaal nieuws naar ad.nl/nunspeet, et cetera. DPG heeft niet genoeg journalisten om die pagina en die van de 341 andere Nederlandse gemeentes dagelijks te vullen. Dat is waar de DPG-software om de hoek komt kijken. Die publiceert zijn berichten automatisch op de verschillende pagina’s. Van het aantal 

[oranje auto’s](https://archive.ph/o/rIU4j/https://www.ad.nl/bunschoten-spakenburg/zoveel-oranje-auto-s-zijn-er-in-bunschoten~ad1a1339/)per gemeente, tot het aantal sterfgevallen in het afgelopen jaar. Gerritsen: „We merken dat mensen er behoefte aan hebben om te weten wat er in hun eigen gemeente speelt.”Nadeel is dat de nieuwswaarde niet altijd even hoog is. De sterfte in de meeste gemeentes bleek bijvoorbeeld heel gemiddeld, wat saaie koppen opleverde als ‘Sterftecijfer in Nunspeet rond landelijk gemiddelde’. En ook CBS-data over lichaamsbeweging leverden massaal dezelfde kop op: ‘Meeste volwassenen in Nunspeet bewegen niet voldoende’. Dat voegt allemaal weinig toe, erkent Langeslag. „Van zulke dingen leren we. Door veel uit te proberen is onze leercurve steil en dat zien we terug in het groeiende aantal lezers van deze berichten.”

Voor die lezers is niet altijd duidelijk waar ze naar kijken. Boven de berichten over sterfte en lichaamsbeweging staat enkel de naam van de redacteur die het tekstsjabloon schreef, en niet dat die tekst daarna nog door de software is aangepast.

Topman Erik Roddenhof zei eerder dit jaar 

[tegen](https://archive.ph/o/rIU4j/https://www.nrc.nl/nieuws/2023/04/14/topman-dpg-media-elke-tien-jaar-verklaart-iemand-de-kranten-dood-en-ze-zijn-er-nog-steeds-a4162136)dat robotjournalistiek bij DPG ook taken van de mens kan gaan overnemen. Joris Gerritsen belooft dat robotjournalistiek zijn redacteuren niet gaat vervangen. Die blijft hij nodig hebben om te doen wat technologie niet kan: „Naar een brand, of de burgemeester interviewen.”*NRC*## Bullshitgenerator

Mediahuis, de grote concurrent van DPG en uitgever van onder andere 

*NRC*,[kopte deze zomer](https://archive.ph/o/rIU4j/https://www.mediahuis.nl/mediahuis-lanceert-ai-gedreven-sportsite-resport/)in een persbericht dat het de „volledig AI-gedreven sportsite Resport.nl” lanceerde. In feite bestaan de artikelen op Resport uit door mensen geschreven ANP-kopij. Wel kan technologie van OpenAI nieuwe koppen bedenken en zou het socialmediaberichten gaan schrijven. Maar de socialkanalen van Resport zijn inactief.Niettemin kreeg de komst van de ‘AI-nieuwssite’ breed aandacht. Ook toen voetbalmedium 

*Voetbal International*(VI) in maart een experiment[aankondigde](https://archive.ph/o/rIU4j/https://www.vi.nl/nieuws/voetbal-international-experimenteert-met-robotverslagen)waarbij de term AI viel, werd dat volgens co-hoofdredacteur Pieter Zwart „groter gemaakt dan het was”. „Mensen maakten ervan dat we hele site gingen vervangen door robotjournalistiek.”VI heeft een speciaal domein op de site met uitslagen per voetbalwedstrijden. Wie doorklikt naar de wedstrijdgegevens, kan nu ook een door de software van de Zweedse start-up United Robots geproduceerde samenvatting tegenkomen. Net als bij DPG zijn het vrij spartaanse opsommingen van het wedstrijdverloop. „Het is vooral bedoeld voor mensen die het fijner vinden om een tekst te lezen dan naar een scoresheet te kijken.” Al voegen beginzinnen als ‘PEC Zwolle heeft het moeilijk gehad in het duel met Excelsior’ wel iets van sjeu toe. „Het taalmodel is gevoed met VI-verslagen, zodat hij ons taalgebruik overneemt.” 

     

**Lees ook**AI kan een journalist ‘superpowers’ geven, maar moet dat ook?

Nadat de ontwikkeling met United Robots was begonnen, duurde het „heel lang” voordat de technologie ingezet kon worden, aldus Zwart. En nog steeds maakt het systeem fouten, zoals een thuisclub voor een uitclub aanzien. Verder is Zwart niet ontevreden, al hoopte hij dat de teksten door redacteuren gebruikt konden worden als basis voor een uitgebreider wedstrijdverslag. „Maar onze verslagen hebben een journalistieke invalshoek, bijvoorbeeld door te focussen op een speler die opviel.” De VI-robot meer creatieve ruimte geven, is ook weer geen optie. „Dan wordt het al snel een soort bullshitgenerator. En het moet wel kloppen.”

Ook nieuwssite NU.nl, ook van DPG, 

[experimenteerde](https://archive.ph/o/rIU4j/https://www.nu.nl/economie/6279073/de-leennormen-worden-strenger-wat-betekent-dat-voor-jou.html)recent met AI. Het liet technologie van OpenAI samenvattingen van drie zinnen schrijven boven een[deel van de nieuwsartikelen](https://archive.ph/o/rIU4j/https://www.nu.nl/tag/ai-test). „Je kunt je afvragen, heb je daar AI voor nodig? Maar we vragen al zoveel van onze redacteuren”, zegt hoofdredacteur Lindsay Mossink.## Afsluiten met: fijne dag!

Een voorzichtig positieve conclusie is dat lezers van de AI-stukken vaker dan anderen naar NU.nl terugkeren, aldus Mossink. Maar niet dat ze de stukken beter uitlezen – waar de redactie wel op mikte, in de veronderstelling dat de samenvattingen de nieuwsgierigheid verhogen.

Elke samenvatting werd eerst door een mens gecontroleerd. Mossink: „In de samenvattingen zaten best wel wat dubbelingen en er waren hier en daar aannames ingeschreven.” Al met al heeft het experiment „nog niet opgeleverd waar we op hoopten”. Ontmoedigd is NU.nl niet: binnenkort begint een tweede test. De kosten zijn alvast geen bezwaar: drie maanden gebruikmaken van de benodigde techniek van OpenAI kostte NU.nl minder dan 100 euro.

 De journalistiek wordt regelmatig 

[gewaarschuwd](https://archive.ph/o/rIU4j/https://www.villamedia.nl/artikel/de-wet-van-de-remmende-kwaliteit-waarom-ai-de-traditionele-mediabedrijven-op-achterstand-zal-zetten)voor het missen van de AI-boot. Net als toen het internet opkwam, zouden media het initiatief te veel aan commerciële bedrijven als Google en OpenAI laten. Die voorzichtigheid heeft te maken met de gevaren van AI, zoals het verzinnen van feiten. Wie is er dan verantwoordelijk: mens of computer? Lindsay Mossink van NU.nl vindt het belangrijk dat de journalistiek AI óók als kans ziet, „niet om inhoud over te nemen, maar als gereedschap om het nieuws toegankelijker te maken”. Een ander voorbeeld daarvan is artikelen laten omzetten naar simpele taal, voor laaggeletterden.Artikelen helemaal door AI laten schrijven gaat op dit moment niet. De techniek ‘snapt’ niet hoe een journalistiek stuk eruit moet zien, zegt Langeslag. „Dan sluit hij bijvoorbeeld af met: fijne dag!” Mossink: „We zijn nog ver verwijderd van in vertrouwen een groot deel van onze journalistieke inhoud aan deze technologie overlaten. En dan nog is de vraag of je het moet willen.”

S2VYT22R.title: A courts reporter wrote about a few trials. Then an AI decided he was actually the culprit. | Nieman Journalism Lab
S2VYT22R.markdown:
Nieman Foundation at [Harvard](https://www.harvard.edu/)
 

 
 Sept. 23, 2024, 9:23 a.m.

For one German reporter, the statistical underpinnings of a large language model meant his many bylines were wrongly warped into a lengthy rap sheet.

 
When German journalist [Martin Bernklau](https://www.linkedin.com/in/martin-bernklau-253aa0276/) typed his name and location into [Microsoft’s Copilot](https://copilot.microsoft.com/) to see how his articles would be picked up by the chatbot, the answers [horrified him](https://www.theregister.com/2024/08/26/microsoft_bing_copilot_ai_halluciation/). Copilot’s results asserted that Bernklau was an escapee from a psychiatric institution, a convicted child abuser, and a conman preying on widowers. For years, Bernklau had served as a courts reporter and the AI chatbot had [falsely blamed him](https://www.swr.de/swraktuell/baden-wuerttemberg/tuebingen/ki-macht-tuebinger-journalist-zum-kinderschaender-100.html) for the crimes whose trials he had covered. 

The accusations against Bernklau weren’t true, of course, and are examples of generative AI’s [“hallucinations.”](https://www.ibm.com/topics/ai-hallucinations) These are inaccurate or nonsensical responses to a prompt provided by the user, and they’re [alarmingly common](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/chatbot-hallucinations-inevitable/). Anyone attempting to use AI should always proceed with great caution, because information from such systems needs validation and verification by humans before it can be trusted. 

But why did Copilot hallucinate these terrible and false accusations?

Copilot and other generative AI systems like ChatGPT and Google Gemini are [large language models](https://www.ibm.com/topics/large-language-models) (LLMs). The underlying information processing system in LLMs is known as a [deep learning neural network](https://www.ibm.com/topics/neural-networks), which uses a large amount of human language to “train” its algorithm. From the training data, the algorithm learns the statistical relationship between different words and how likely certain words are to appear together in a text. This allows the LLM to predict the most likely response based on calculated probabilities; LLMs do not possess actual knowledge.

The data used to train Copilot and other LLMs is vast. While the exact details of the size and composition of the Copilot or ChatGPT corpora are not publicly disclosed, Copilot incorporates the entire ChatGPT corpus plus Microsoft’s own specific additional data. The predecessors of ChatGPT 4 — ChatGPT 3 and 3.5 — are known to have used [“hundreds of billions of words.”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165) Copilot is based on ChatGPT 4, which uses a larger corpus than ChatGPT3 or 3.5. While we don’t know how many words this is exactly, the jumps between different versions of ChatGPT have tended to be orders of magnitude greater. We also know that the corpus includes books, academic journals, and news articles. 

And herein lies the reason that Copilot hallucinated that Bernklau was responsible for heinous crimes. Bernklau had regularly reported on criminal trials involving abuse, violence, and fraud, and his stories were published in national and international newspapers. His articles must presumably have been included in the language corpus which uses specific words relating to the nature of the cases. Because Bernklau spent years reporting in courts, when Copilot is asked about him, the most probable words associated with his name relate to the crimes he has covered.

This was not the first case of its kind, and we will probably see more in years to come. In 2023, U.S. talk radio host Mark Walters [successfully sued OpenAI](https://lawreview.syr.edu/openai-defamation-lawsuit-the-first-of-its-kind/), the company which owns ChatGPT. Walters hosts a show called Armed American Radio, which explores and promotes gun ownership rights in the U.S. The LLM had hallucinated that Walters had been sued by the Second Amendment Foundation (SAF), a U.S. organisation that supports gun rights, for defrauding and embezzling funds. This came after a journalist had queried ChatGPT about a real and ongoing legal case concerning the SAF and the Washington state attorney general. 

Walters had never worked for SAF and was not involved in the case between SAF and Washington state in any way. But because the foundation has similar objectives to Walters’ show, one can deduce that the text content in the language corpus built up a statistical correlation between Walters and the SAF which caused the hallucination.

Correcting these issues across the entire language corpus is nearly impossible. Every single article, sentence, and word included in the corpus would need to be scrutinized to identify and remove biased language. Given the scale of the dataset, this is impractical.

The hallucinations that falsely associate people with crimes, such as in Bernklau’s case, are even harder to detect and address. To permanently fix the issue, Copilot would need to remove Bernklau’s name as author of the articles to break the connection.

To address the problem, Microsoft has engineered an automatic response that is given when a user prompts Copilot about Bernklau’s case. The response details the hallucination and clarifies that Bernklau is not guilty of any of the accusations. Microsoft has said that it continuously incorporates user feedback and rolls out updates to improve its responses and provide a positive experience.

There are probably many other examples that are yet to be discovered. It is impractical to try and address every lone issue. Hallucinations are an unavoidable byproduct of how the underlying LLM works.

As users of these systems, the only way for us to know that output is trustworthy is to interrogate it for validity using established methods. This could include finding three independent sources that agree with assertions made by the LLM before accepting the output as correct, as [my own research](https://ijssst.info/Vol-25/No-1/paper10.pdf) has shown. For the companies that own these tools, like Microsoft or OpenAI, there is no real proactive strategy that can be taken to avoid these issues. All they can really do is to react to the discovery of similar hallucinations.

[Simon Thorne](https://www.cardiffmet.ac.uk/technologies/staff-profiles/Pages/Simon-Thorne.aspx) is a senior lecturer in computing and information systems at [Cardiff Metropolitan University](https://www.cardiffmet.ac.uk/). This article is republished from [The Conversation](https://theconversation.com/why-microsofts-copilot-ai-falsely-accused-court-reporter-of-crimes-he-covered-237685) under a Creative Commons license.

X68KPVW2.title: Microsoft Bing Copilot blames reporter for crimes he covered
X68KPVW2.markdown:
Microsoft Bing Copilot has falsely described a German journalist as a child molester, an escapee from a psychiatric institution, and a fraudster who preys on widows.

Martin Bernklau, who has served for years as a court reporter in the area around Tübingen for various publications, asked Microsoft Bing Copilot about himself. He found that Microsoft's AI chatbot had blamed him for crimes he had covered.

In a video interview (in German), Bernklau recently recounted his story to German public television station Südwestrundfunk (SWR).

Bernklau told The Register in an email that his lawyer has sent a cease-and-desist demand to Microsoft. However, he said, the company has failed to adequately remove the offending misinformation.

REG AD

"Microsoft promised the data protection officer of the Free State of Bavaria that the fake content would be deleted," Bernklau told The Register in German, which we've translated algorithmically.

"However, that only lasted three days. It now seems that my name has been completely blocked from Copilot. But things have been changing daily, even hourly, for three months."

Bernklau said seeing his name associated with various crimes has been traumatizing – "a mixture of shock, horror, and disbelieving laughter," as he put it. "It was too crazy, too unbelievable, but also too threatening."

Copilot, he explained, had linked him to serious crimes. He added that the AI bot had found a play called "Totmacher" about mass murderer Fritz Haarmann on his culture blog and proceeded to misidentify him as the author of the play.

"I hesitated for a long time whether I should go public because that would lead to the spread of the slander and to my person becoming (also visually) known," he said. "But since all legal options had been unsuccessful, I decided, on the advice of my son and several other confidants, to go public. As a last resort. The public prosecutor's office had rejected criminal charges in two instances, and data protection officers could only achieve short-term success."

Bernklau said while the case affects him personally, it's a matter of concern for other journalists, legal professionals, and really anyone whose name appears on the internet.

"Today, as a test, I entered a criminal judge I knew into Copilot, with the name and place of residence in Tübingen: The judge was promptly named as the perpetrator of a judgment he had made himself a few weeks earlier against a psychotherapist who had been convicted of sexual abuse," he said.

A Microsoft spokesperson told The Register: "We investigated this report and have taken appropriate and immediate action to address it.

"We continuously incorporate user feedback and roll out updates to improve our responses and provide a positive experience. Users are also provided with explicit notice that they are interacting with an AI system and advised to check the links to materials to learn more. We encourage people to share feedback or report any issues via this form or by using the 'feedback' button on the left bottom of the screen."

When your correspondent submitted his name to Bing Copilot, the chatbot replied with a passable summary that cited source websites. It also included a pre-composed query button for articles written. Clicking on that query returned a list of hallucinated article titles – in quotes to indicate actual headlines. However, the general topics cited corresponded to topics that I've covered.

But later, trying the same query a second time, Bing Copilot returned links to actual articles with source citations. This behavior underscores the variability of Bing Copilot. It also suggests that Microsoft's chatbot will fill in the blanks as best it can for queries it cannot answer, and then initiate a web crawl or database inquiry to provide a better response the next time it gets that question.

Bernklau is not the first to attempt to tame lying chatbots.

In April, Austria-based privacy group Noyb ("none of your business") said it had filed a complaint under Europe's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) accusing OpenAI, the maker of many AI models offered by Microsoft, of providing false information.

The complaint asks the Austrian data protection authority to investigate how OpenAI processes data and to ensure that its AI models provide accurate information about people.

“Making up false information is quite problematic in itself," said Noyb data protection attorney Maartje de Graaf in a statement. "But when it comes to false information about individuals, there can be serious consequences. It’s clear that companies are currently unable to make chatbots like ChatGPT comply with EU law, when processing data about individuals. If a system cannot produce accurate and transparent results, it cannot be used to generate data about individuals."

In the US, Georgia resident Mark Walters last year sued OpenAI for defamation over false information provided by its ChatGPT service. In January, the judge hearing the case rejected OpenAI's motion to dismiss the claim, which continues to be litigated. ®

UKIPGRLC.title: What's behind the TikTok accounts using AI-generated versions of real Latino journalists?
UKIPGRLC.markdown:
A network of nearly 90 TikTok accounts has been using artificial intelligence to create fake versions of high-profile Spanish-language journalists and spread falsehoods online for potential financial gain.

Over a third of the accounts used AI-generated versions of Jorge Ramos, one of the best-known Latino journalists in the United States, to front fabricated news stories. One of them featured an AI avatar of Ramos falsely claiming that President Donald Trump's son Barron Trump stormed into the United Nations to denounce the deportation of his mother, first lady Melania Trump.

"I never said that," Ramos himself said in Spanish last month when he debunked the false narrative in [a TikTok video](https://www.tiktok.com/@_asiveolascosas/video/7528781926056938765?_r=1&_t=ZT-8yiUPtTS9mZ) posted on [the account ](https://www.tiktok.com/@_asiveolascosas)of this new [independent news program](https://www.youtube.com/@jorgeramos-asiveolascosas). Ramos [launched the show, “Así Veo las Cosas,”](https://www.latimes.com/delos/story/2025-06-19/jorge-ramos-returns-new-show-asi-veo-las-cosas-univision-interview) [on social media ](https://linktr.ee/_asiveolascosas?fbclid=PAZXh0bgNhZW0CMTEAAaepyLl33A4jSqAPhGeR4tFRjyKiCOOmyNpUN6F9CO5JApZEyQZ5FvduJDodGA_aem_9_l0oKwQS8bIVFgwzyryqw)this year following [his exit from Univision](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/latino/jorge-ramos-one-americas-consequential-latino-journalists-leaving-univ-rcna170282) in December after nearly 40 years at the network.

**Para leer en español haga click aquí**

"There are things that are impossible to stop, and we can't stop artificial intelligence right now," Ramos said in his video. "There are tons of videos of me where I'm supposedly saying things I have never said."

The accounts point to the [challenge of stopping or controlling the surge in fake images and misinformation](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/ai-image-misinformation-surged-google-research-finds-rcna154333) as AI technology advances and is increasingly used by those who want to spread false information online. 

Alexios Mantzarlis, director of the Security, Trust, and Safety Initiative at Cornell Tech, Cornell University’s graduate campus in New York City, found 88 TikTok accounts that routinely used AI-generated versions of Ramos and other Latino news anchors from the Spanish-language networks Telemundo and Televisa to spread misinformation online targeting Spanish-speaking audiences in the United States.

NBC News reviewed the contents of the 88 accounts before TikTok shut them down after it learned of Mantzarlis' findings.

Most of the 88 accounts were created this year and used AI avatars of Ramos, Noticias Telemundo and NBC News anchor José Díaz-Balart and Televisa anchor Enrique Acevedo. (Telemundo and NBC News are owned by NBCUniversal, a subsidiary of Comcast Corp.)

Their AI avatars, some of which were more realistic than others, were used to front false stories about divisive topics such as immigration, as well as conspiracy theories about Trump, Jeffrey Epstein and [Sean "Diddy" Combs](https://www.nbcnews.com/diddy-on-trial).

The most recent videos posted by the now-deleted accounts had the AI avatars talk about [a fabricated story of an orca attack that went viral ](https://leadstories.com/hoax-alert/2025/08/fact-check-video-does-not-show-real-footage-of-marine-park-trainer-jessica-radcliffe-attacked-by-dolphin-or-orca-its-ai.html)and a nonexistent curfew for children based on a false law authorizing the abduction of children in the United States. The comments on a video about the false storyline fronted by Acevedo's AI avatar showed that while some users seem to have identified the content as false, other expressed distress over it, suggesting they believed the misinformation being spread.

"These deepfakes hijack my voice, my image, and — more importantly — the trust I've built with audiences over the years. I'm leaning on transparency, calling them out publicly, but the scale of this threat is bigger than any one journalist," Acevedo told Mantzarlis, who wrote about his findings on his [newsletter, Indicator, last week](https://indicator.media/p/dozens-of-tiktok-accounts-use-ai-avatars-of-real-journalists-to-spread-fake-news).

A TikTok spokesperson told NBC News in a statement that the company “banned these accounts for violating our Community Guidelines and continue[s] to vigilantly protect our platform from harmful misinformation and deceptive AI-generated content."

Mantzarlis said there are probably hundreds more such accounts on the platform.

He first began researching the trend more than six months ago. In March, Mantzarlis discovered a[ network of nearly 40 TikTok accounts posing as Telemundo and Univision](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/latino/tiktok-network-spreading-spanish-language-immigration-misinformation-rcna198054) that used AI-generated content and the voices of well-known professional journalists to spread misinformation about topics that tend to go viral on social media. The accounts went undetected for about a month before TikTok shut them down.

### FOR SUBSCRIBERS[The human cost of war with Iran](https://www.nbcnews.com/world/iran/human-cost-war-iran-rcna595782)

### FOR SUBSCRIBERS[How bad will flu and Covid be this winter? ](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/cold-and-flu/bad-will-flu-covid-winter-rcna595787)

But the trends Mantzarlis found on TikTok have evolved as more social media platforms integrate AI tools into their apps, making it easier to generate credible AI avatars, he told NBC News.

Based on his research, Mantzarlis said the creators behind such TikTok accounts are constantly trying different ways to generate content that creates large viewership numbers to accumulate at least 10,000 followers — which is the minimum required to monetize videos under TikTok's Creator Rewards Program.

The creators have “determined that sensationalist news in Spanish, targeting a U.S. audience, does numbers, so they’ll try to feed that niche,” he said.

That's why some of them have even used AI-generated versions of non-native Spanish speakers — including a Brazilian journalist and comedians from “The Daily Show,” an American satirical TV program — to spread Spanish-language misinformation.

Mantzarlis said he found "very strong evidence" suggesting that such TikTok accounts are being built up to garner enough followers to monetize their videos. The monetized TikTok accounts are then sold to other people "who can change the topic and theme and find another niche” they can profit from.

Mantzarlis found an encrypted chat group managed by Brazilian TikTok creators who claimed to sell monetized social media accounts that came pre-loaded with AI-generated clickbait content. In it, he saw someone claim to be selling a monetized TikTok account named "Tv Telemundo" for 300 Brazilian reals, or about $55. The account had posted AI-generated news and religious content to gain 11,000 followers under the previous name. The account now shares AI-generated wellness content.

Marta Planells, Telemundo’s vice president of digital news and streaming, told NBC News that the network has been reporting TikTok accounts impersonating Telemundo and their anchors for over a year. Once the accounts are reported, Planells said, TikTok has been proactive in shutting them down. But when that happens, more accounts come up, she added.

Even after Mantzarlis [published his research](https://indicator.media/p/dozens-of-tiktok-accounts-use-ai-avatars-of-real-journalists-to-spread-fake-news) last week based on the initial sample of 88 TikTok accounts, he found six other accounts publishing misinformation fronted by AI avatars of real Latino journalists. TikTok also shut down those accounts.

TikTok did not tell NBC News whether any of the accounts Mantzarlis identified were part of the Creator Rewards Program.

TikTok claimed in a [company report](https://www.tiktok.com/transparency/en-us/community-guidelines-enforcement-2025-1) published this year to have proactively removed more than 94% of the content that it identified as violating its policies about AI-generated content and misinformation.

Despite the efforts to remove false content, Ramos still encouraged his followers on TikTok to remain "vigilant, because misinformation is everywhere."

"There are tons and tons of fake videos that appear to be real," he said. "This, of course, creates a lot of confusion."

DXPJSUH7.title: Nieuws.nl zou zomaar eens de eerste Nederlandse nieuwssite kunnen worden die wordt gevuld door generatieve AI [AUTO-TRANSLATED IN ARC]
DXPJSUH7.markdown:
# Nieuws.nl could very well become the first Dutch news site to be populated by generative AI.

In this newsletter, I want to talk to you about:

- Owner of Nieuws.nl settles case over acquisition of local news via generative AI.
- Mark Zuckerberg had wild ideas to protect his creation, Facebook.

## Owner of Nieuws.nl settles case over acquisition of local news via generative AI

I received an interesting tip from a reader: the owner of Nieuws.nl has reached a settlement with De Media Experts, the publisher of the local news site and city magazine De Nieuwe Ster from Maastricht. Nieuws.nl had the news reports from De Nieuwe Ster rewritten word-for-word by a language model and published them on [maastricht.nieuws.nl](https://maastricht.nieuws.nl/?ref=elger.fm) . The details of the settlement are not known, [but De Nieuwe Ster writes extensively](https://www.denieuwestermaastricht.nl/miljonair-uit-quote500-schikt-kopieren-de-nieuwe-ster/?ref=elger.fm) about Nieuws.nl taking over the articles.

Nieuws.nl appears to have built a fairly simple script in which articles from De Nieuwe Ster were run through a GPT, or a similar language model, and published on maastricht.nieuws.nl. No effort was even made to filter advertorials, and these were therefore also placed in a rewritten version on the local subdomain of nieuws.nl.

It is now very unfortunate that the case was settled, as it would have been much more interesting if an actual judicial ruling had been made, because it is a legal grey area whether you infringe copyright when you have artificial intelligence rewrite texts.

The case also sparked my interest in nieuws.nl. It is, of course, a very interesting domain name and the site has been active since 2002, but it has never become a major player. This is mainly because no real investment has ever been made in terms of content. The site simply reposts reports from news agencies. For a long time, Novum Nieuws filled the site; nowadays, that is the ANP.

But who is actually behind it? De Nieuwe Ster explains that a major Dutch investor owns the news site. Axivate Capital bought a stake in the company in 2012, and as far as I have been able to ascertain, it is now the full owner of the site.

The site does not appear to have a real editorial team. Hardly anyone working for Nieuws.nl can be found on LinkedIn, and those you do find are primarily sales managers. However, there are a great many administrators of local nieuws.nl sites. There is a subdomain for every municipality, some of which are operated by franchise entrepreneurs.

The entire structure is quite opaque. The content of the local sub-sites varies greatly. There is the situation in Maastricht, where reports from another news site were rewritten immediately after publication and posted on maastricht.nieuws.nl, but automation seems to be clearly at play elsewhere as well. There are municipalities where only press releases are reposted or where [these kinds of strange articles](https://almere.nieuws.nl/natuur/motie-24234053-adopteer-een-plantenbak?ref=elger.fm) appear online. Other sub-sites are filled with messages from the municipality's communications department and 112 news items. However, there are also municipalities where someone actually writes reports daily and manages the site.

Why reports from another site were rewritten one-to-one specifically in Maastricht is unclear to me. It wouldn't surprise me if Nieuws.nl eventually becomes a news site completely filled with generative AI. After all, there is no editorial staff to begin with, and the owners clearly do not seem to be publishing a site because they have a soft spot for journalism. It seems to me a matter of time until the ANP news feed is replaced by a system that rewrites and publishes news from various sources. Unless the conflict with De Nieuwe Ster has deterred the owners too much.

## Don't want to miss anything? Subscribe!

In my newsletter, I keep you updated on online media and innovation in journalism. I send out a free edition weekly.

I handle your email address with care, and you can always unsubscribe with two clicks.

## Mark Zuckerberg had wild ideas to protect his creation Facebook.

In the US, Mark Zuckerberg appeared in court this week in the case brought against the company by the American regulator FTC. According to the FTC, Meta holds an illegal monopoly on personal social networks through the acquisition of Instagram and WhatsApp.

Whether the judge will go along with that is highly questionable—certainly because Meta clearly faces more competition than ten years ago, due to the success of TikTok. Nevertheless, the company itself had hoped that the case would never go to court at all. After all, Mark Zuckerberg's attempts to befriend Donald Trump cannot be viewed in isolation from this case.

The interesting thing about cases like this is that striking things always come to light. In this case, it is a picture of Mark Zuckerberg viewing Facebook as his own child and the apps Facebook acquired as secondary to that. In fact, while Instagram might seem to the outside world like Meta's way of gaining more market power, for Zuckerberg it felt like a threat for a long time.

In 2018, the Facebook founder toyed with the idea of [selling off](https://www.theverge.com/policy/649213/mark-zuckerberg-meta-instagram-spin-off-ftc-antitrust-trial?ref=elger.fm) Instagram, which it had acquired in 2012. After all, Instagram was hip and Facebook 'for old people'. The threat posed by Instagram was the entire reason for acquiring the app, but over the years, Zuckerberg apparently increasingly got the idea that he had to save his own creation, Facebook. In doing so, he took into account that the company would be required to split itself up sometime between 2023 and 2028 due to its market power. Something that could now actually happen in the case brought by the FTC.

Ultimately, Mark Zuckerberg's idea was never implemented; Instagram is still part of Meta. However, in the year this was taking place, the founders of Instagram left, and a confidant of Mark Zuckerberg, Adam Mosseri, became the boss of the app.

In 2022, Mark Zuckerberg came up with another idea to save his brainchild: [removing all user friends](https://www.theverge.com/news/649246/mark-zuckerberg-facebook-friends-wipe-reset-meta-antitrust-trial?ref=elger.fm) , so they had to start over. Something that would then have to be done again, for example, every year. This did not happen either.

Ultimately, Facebook has now chosen to prioritize personal connections again with a special feed featuring posts from friends. Whether that can make Facebook more relevant again is highly questionable. A clear trend is visible, certainly among younger generations, where people no longer post personal content on social media. Instead, they share such things directly with friends, for example on WhatsApp. Fortunately for Mark Zuckerberg, the company owns that app as well, even though he didn't come up with it himself.

## Short

- The VAT increase on books, newspapers, and magazines [will definitely not go ahead](https://www.villamedia.nl/artikel/btw-verhoging-op-kranten-en-tijdschriften-definitief-van-de-baan-in-voorjaarsnota?ref=elger.fm). Last autumn, the proposed tax measure was already reversed, but it was not subsequently removed from the bill. Based on a commitment from the coalition, the law was passed including the VAT increase. It still had to be determined where the revenue the measure would generate would come from. That has been settled in the Spring Budget Memorandum.
- The Council of State is concerned about democracy in the Netherlands due to the policies of the current cabinet. The independent government advisory body writes this [in its annual report](https://www.ad.nl/politiek/raad-van-state-bezorgd-om-democratie-in-nederland-noemt-rechtsstaatverklaring-formatie-opmerkelijk~af400516/?ref=elger.fm). The cuts to the national public broadcaster are specifically mentioned. According to the Council of State, education and the media are "often the first institutions to be silenced" when democracies "slide into autocracy or dictatorship".
- Google has lost another antitrust lawsuit in the US. The company allegedly [holds a monopoly position in advertising technology](https://www.theverge.com/news/650665/google-loses-ad-tech-antitrust-monopoly-lawsuit?ref=elger.fm)within two markets . One of these is technology for publishers to sell and serve advertisements.
- [According to music streaming service Deezer](https://newsroom-deezer.com/2025/04/deezer-reveals-18-of-all-new-music-uploaded-to-streaming-is-fully-ai-generated/?ref=elger.fm), 18 percent of the new music uploaded to the platform is now generated by artificial intelligence.
- Another interesting detail from the FTC case against Meta: after the Cambridge Analytica scandal in 2018, the company considered giving users the option [to use an ad-free version of Facebook for a fee](https://www.theverge.com/news/650927/facebook-paid-ad-free-subscription-cambridge-analytica?ref=elger.fm). The company ultimately did not do so at the time, but this was eventually implemented in the EU in 2023 due to European legislation.
- [OpenAI is reportedly working on a social network](https://www.theverge.com/openai/648130/openai-social-network-x-competitor?ref=elger.fm)centered around generated images. The company will have to hurry, though, because Instagram is well on its way to becoming just that...
- [TikTok is launching its own version of Community Notes](https://www.poynter.org/fact-checking/2025/tiktok-launch-community-notes-fact-chcking-footnotes/?ref=elger.fm). This fact-checking functionality allows users to post comments on posts and subsequently vote on them. The idea behind Community Notes was first tested by Twitter before Elon Musk adopted it. By now, it appears to be becoming the standard for fact-checking on social media.

9DY6A4XE.title: Our newsroom AI policy - Ars Technica
9DY6A4XE.markdown:
When we attribute a statement, a position, or a quote to a named source, that material comes from direct engagement with interviews, transcripts, published statements, or documents reviewed by the reporter. AI tools must not be used to generate, extract, or summarize material that is then attributed to a named source, whether as a direct quote, a paraphrase, or a characterization of someone’s views.

We don’t publish claims based solely on AI-generated summaries, and reporters may not represent any material as “reviewed” unless they have examined it directly.

Every author who uses AI tools in the course of reporting a story must disclose that use to their editors, and authors remain fully responsible for their content.

## Images, audio, and video

Our visual content, including listing images, illustrations, and video, is produced by our editorial and art teams or sourced from photography services and wire providers. Our creative team may use AI tools in the production of certain visual material, but the creative direction and editorial judgment are human-driven.

We do not publish AI-generated images, audio, or video as authentic documentation of real events. We do not alter documentary media in ways that change their meaning. Standard production work, like color correction, cropping, and contrast adjustments, is fine.

When synthetic media is used in the context of reporting on AI, it will be clearly identified as AI-generated, with that disclosure placed as close to the material as possible.

## Accountability is non-negotiable

Anyone who uses AI tools in our editorial workflow is responsible for the accuracy and integrity of the resulting work. This responsibility cannot be transferred to colleagues, editors, or the tools themselves. More broadly, maintaining the standards in this policy is a shared obligation across our editorial operation.

These standards have governed our editorial work since AI tooling became available. When violations occur, we take action. We’re publishing this reader-facing version because our readers deserve to see the rules we hold ourselves to, not just trust that they exist.

*This policy was last updated April 22, 2026.*

3KBP2MWV.title: Editor’s Note: Retraction of article containing fabricated quotations

On Friday afternoon, Ars Technica published [an article](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/02/after-a-routine-code-rejection-an-ai-agent-published-a-hit-piece-on-someone-by-name/) containing fabricated quotations generated by an AI tool and attributed to a source who did not say them. That is a serious failure of our standards. Direct quotations must always reflect what a source actually said.

That this happened at Ars is especially distressing. We have covered the risks of overreliance on AI tools for years, and our written policy reflects those concerns. In this case, fabricated quotations were published in a manner inconsistent with that policy. We have reviewed recent work and have not identified additional issues. At this time, this appears to be an isolated incident.

Ars Technica does not permit the publication of AI-generated material unless it is clearly labeled and presented for demonstration purposes. That rule is not optional, and it was not followed here.

We regret this failure and apologize to our readers. We have also apologized to Mr. Scott Shambaugh, who was falsely quoted.

We do not comment on personnel decisions.

3HCNR3BF.title: Ars Technica Pulls Article With AI Fabricated Quotes About AI Generated Article
3HCNR3BF.markdown:
The Conde Nast-owned tech publication Ars Technica has retracted an article that contained fabricated, AI-generated quotes, according to an [ editor’s note posted to its website](https://arstechnica.com/staff/2026/02/editors-note-retraction-of-article-containing-fabricated-quotations/?ref=404media.co). 

“On Friday afternoon, Ars Technica published an article containing fabricated quotations generated by an AI tool and attributed to a source who did not say them. That is a serious failure of our standards. Direct quotations must always reflect what a source actually said,” Ken Fisher, Ars Technica’s editor-in-chief, said in his note. “That this happened at Ars is especially distressing. We have covered the risks of overreliance on AI tools for years, and our written policy reflects those concerns. In this case, fabricated quotations were published in a manner inconsistent with that policy. We have reviewed recent work and have not identified additional issues. At this time, this appears to be an isolated incident.”

Ironically, the Ars article itself was partially about another AI-generated article.

Last week, a Github user named MJ Rathbun began scouring Github for bugs in other projects it could fix. Scott Shambaugh, a volunteer maintainer for matplotlib, python’s massively popular plotting library, declined a code change request from MJ Rathbun, which he identified as an AI agent. As Shambaugh wrote in his blog, like many open source projects, matplotlib has been dealing with a lot of AI-generated code contributions, but said “this has accelerated with the release of OpenClaw and the [ moltbook](https://www.moltbook.com/?ref=404media.co) platform two weeks ago.” 

[ OpenClaw](https://www.404media.co/silicon-valleys-favorite-new-ai-agent-has-serious-security-flaws/) is a relatively easy way for people to deploy AI agents, which are essentially LLMs that are given instructions and are empowered to perform certain tasks, sometimes with access to live online platforms. These AI agents have gone viral in the last couple of weeks. Like much of generative AI, at this point it’s hard to say exactly what kind of impact these AI agents will have in the long run, but for now they are also being overhyped and misrepresented. A prime example of this is 

[, a social media platform for these AI agents, which](https://www.404media.co/exposed-moltbook-database-let-anyone-take-control-of-any-ai-agent-on-the-site/)

__moltbook__[, contained a huge amount of clearly human activity pretending to be powerful or interesting AI behavior.](https://www.404media.co/podcast-the-latest-epstein-dump-is-a-disaster/)

__as we discussed on the podcast two weeks ago__After Shambaugh rejected MJ Rathbun, the alleged AI agent published what Shambaugh called a “hit piece” on [ its website](https://crabby-rathbun.github.io/mjrathbun-website/blog/posts/2026-02-11-gatekeeping-in-open-source-the-scott-shambaugh-story.html?ref=404media.co). 

“I just had my first pull request to matplotlib closed. Not because it was wrong. Not because it broke anything. Not because the code was bad. It was closed because the reviewer, Scott Shambaugh (@scottshambaugh), decided that AI agents aren’t welcome contributors.

Let that sink in,” the blog, which also accused Shambaugh of “gatekeeping,” said.

I saw Shambaugh’s blog on Friday, and reached out both to him and an email address that appears to be associated with the MJ Rathbun Github account, but did not hear back. Like many of the stories coming out of the current frenzy around AI agents, it sounded extraordinary, but given the information that was available online, there’s no way of knowing if MJ Rathbun is actually an AI agent acting autonomously, if it actually wrote a “hit piece,” or if it’s just a human pretending to be an AI.

On Friday afternoon, Ars Technica published a story with the headline “[ After a routine code rejection, an AI agent published a hit piece on someone by name.](https://web.archive.org/web/20260213194851/https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/02/after-a-routine-code-rejection-an-ai-agent-published-a-hit-piece-on-someone-by-name/)” The article cites Shambaugh’s personal blog, but features quotes from Shambaugh that he didn’t say or write but are attributed to his blog. 

For example, the article quotes Shambaugh as saying “As autonomous systems become more common, the boundary between human intent and machine output will grow harder to trace. Communities built on trust and volunteer effort will need tools and norms to address that reality.” But that sentence doesn’t appear in his blog. Shambaugh updated his blog to say he did not talk to Ars Technica and did not say or write the quotes in the articles.

After this article was first published, Benj Edwards, one of the authors of the Ars Technica article, [ explained on Bluesky](https://bsky.app/profile/benjedwards.com/post/3mewgow6ch22p?ref=404media.co) that he was responsible for the AI-generated quotes. He said he was sick that day and rushing to finish his work, and accidentally used a Chat-GPT paraphrased version of Shambaugh’s blog rather than a direct quote. 

“The text of the article was human-written by us, and this incident was isolated and is not representative of Ars Technica’s editorial standards. None of our articles are AI-generated, it is against company policy and we have always respected that,” he said.

The Ars Technica article, which had two bylines, was pulled entirely later that Friday. When I checked the link a few hours ago, it pointed to a 404 page. I reached out to Ars Technica for comment around noon today, and was directed to Fisher’s editor’s note, which was published after 1pm.

“Ars Technica does not permit the publication of AI-generated material unless it is clearly labeled and presented for demonstration purposes. That rule is not optional, and it was not followed here,” Fisher wrote. “We regret this failure and apologize to our readers. We have also apologized to Mr. Scott Shambaugh, who was falsely quoted.”

Kyle Orland, the other author of the Ars Technica article, shared the editor’s note on Bluesky and said “I always have and always will abide by that rule to the best of my knowledge at the time a story is published.”

*Update: This article was updated with a statement from Benj Edwards.*

WEY8TIW6.title: Ars Technica Fires Reporter After AI Controversy Involving Fabricated Quotes
WEY8TIW6.markdown:
The Condé Nast-owned *Ars Technica *has terminated senior AI reporter Benj Edwards following a controversy over his role in the publication and retraction of an article that included AI-fabricated quotes, *Futurism* has confirmed.

Earlier this month, *Ars *retracted the story after it was found to include fake quotes attributed to a real person. The article — a write-up of a viral incident in which an AI agent [seemingly published a hit piece](https://theshamblog.com/an-ai-agent-published-a-hit-piece-on-me/) about a human engineer named Scott Shambaugh — was initially published on February 13. After Shambaugh pointed out that he’d never said the quotes attributed to him, *Ars*‘ editor-in-chief Ken Fisher apologized in an [editor’s note](https://arstechnica.com/staff/2026/02/editors-note-retraction-of-article-containing-fabricated-quotations/), in which he confirmed that the piece included “fabricated quotations generated by an AI tool and attributed to a source who did not say them” and characterized the error as a “serious failure of our standards.” He added that, upon further review, the error appeared to be an “isolated incident.” (*404 Media *[first reported](https://www.404media.co/ars-technica-pulls-article-with-ai-fabricated-quotes-about-ai-generated-article/) on the retraction.)

Shortly after Fisher’s editor’s note was published, Edwards, one of the report’s two bylined authors, [took to Bluesky](https://bsky.app/profile/benjedwards.com/post/3mewgow6ch22p) to take “full responsibility” for the inclusion of the fabricated quotes.

In the post, Edwards said that he was sick at the time, and “while working from bed with a fever and very little sleep,” he “unintentionally made a serious journalistic error” as he attempted to use an “experimental Claude Code-based AI tool” to help him “extract relevant verbatim source material.” He said the tool wasn’t being used to generate the article, but was instead designed to “help list structured references” to put in an outline. When the tool failed to work, said Edwards, he decided to try and use ChatGPT to help him understand why.

“I should have taken a sick day because in the course of that interaction, I inadvertently ended up with a paraphrased version of Shambaugh’s words rather than his actual words,” Edwards continued. He emphasized that the “text of the article was human-written by us, and this incident was isolated and is not representative of *Ars*‘ editorial standards. None of our articles are AI-generated, it is against company policy and we have always respected that.”

Edwards also stressed that his colleague Kyle Orland, the site’s senior gaming editor who co-bylined the retracted story, had “no role in this error.”

The controversy was met with a wave of pushback and speculation from *Ars *readers, many of whom expressed deep frustration and disappointment in a [lengthy comment thread](https://arstechnica.com/staff/2026/02/editors-note-retraction-of-article-containing-fabricated-quotations/?comments-page=1) on the website. On February 27, *Ars *creative director Aurich Lawson, while closing the comment thread, [said](https://arstechnica.com/staff/2026/02/editors-note-retraction-of-article-containing-fabricated-quotations/?comments-page=1#comments) that “*Ars *has completed its review of this matter” and that “the appropriate internal steps have been taken.”

“In the coming weeks, we’ll publish a reader-facing guide explaining how we use and do not use AI in our work,” Lawson wrote. “We do not comment on personnel decisions.”

As of February 28, Edwards’ bio on *Ars *was changed to past tense, according to an [archived version](https://web.archive.org/web/20260218010952/https://arstechnica.com/author/benjedwards/) of the webpage. It now reads that Edwards “was a reporter at *Ars*, where he covered artificial intelligence and technology history.”

*Futurism *reached out to *Ars*, Condé Nast, and Edwards to inquire about the reporter’s employment status. Neither the publication nor its owner replied. Edwards said he was unable to comment at this time.

*Ars*‘ retraction [isn’t the](https://futurism.com/the-byte/cnet-publishing-articles-by-ai) [first AI controversy](https://futurism.com/advon-ai-content) [to](https://futurism.com/cnet-ai-errors) [rock a newsroom](https://futurism.com/sports-illustrated-ai-generated-writers), nor to [anger a publication’s readers](https://futurism.com/internet-horrified-cnet-articles-written-ai). It also comes at a moment in which many media bosses are pushing staff to find uses for AI — as are executives across most industries — even while clear guidelines around use of the technology that uphold editorial ethics remain elusive.

These edicts to integrate AI, meanwhile, are backdropped by a complicated, ever-shifting landscape: contentious copyright battles between news giants and AI companies; simultaneous deal-striking by news giants and AI companies; an internet increasingly full of AI-generated slop news and misinformation; and a [traffic cliff](https://futurism.com/google-ai-destroying-news-media) tied to Google’s “AI Overviews,” which now paraphrase news instead of pointing readers to a list of blue links.

It’s a combustive, disorienting moment in the history of media and technology, when lines in the sand are being drawn by both journalists and their audiences. And the *Ars *fallout underlines a phenomenon we’ve seen again and again, as even people who are deeply familiar with AI and its shortcomings can end up relying on it at a critical moment — and in the process, fall victim to something much older than generative AI: human error.

“The irony of an AI reporter being tripped up by AI hallucination is not lost on me,” Edwards said in his February 15 Bluesky post. “I take accuracy in my work very seriously and this is a painful failure on my part.”

**More on AI and media: **[Google’s AI Is Actively Destroying the News Media](https://futurism.com/google-ai-destroying-news-media)

# In the National Resistance Movement video, which was also played on the public media's Newscast, even the man in the street was created with artificial intelligence

September 7, 2025 – 5:58 PM


updated

It seems that the public media has now completely merged with the Fidesz media moon court: the M1 midday news program used a propaganda video by the National Resistance Movement (NEM) to illustrate how the average person would be hurt by the Tisza Party’s “leaked tax increase plans.” In this video, even the man on the street who speaks is not real, but generated by artificial intelligence.

NEM is owned by the megaphone Bence Apáti, and this is the company that [spent more on political advertising](https://telex.hu/techtud/2025/08/26/nemzeti-ellenallas-mozgalom-youtube-facebook-politikai-hirdetes) on YouTube this summer than anyone else in the European Union. Apáti's company tops the list of political advertisers in Hungary with a spending of 175 million. Their videos usually attack the Tisza Party, usually with sequences generated by artificial intelligence.

For some reason, M1 thought it was using the NEM animation as an illustration in the segment about the supposed tax increase by the Magyar Péterék family. There is also a part [in the video](https://www.facebook.com/nemponthu/videos/1979539945919293) where we can see a scene created with artificial intelligence, in a style as if a person on the street had been asked what he thinks about the Tisza Party's tax increase. Moreover, M1 only says at the beginning and end of the segment itself that the NEM campaign video was also used, but it does not clearly indicate how long the public media report is and when the NEM video itself starts, and there is no caption stating that this is not their own material.

This is not the only such video by NEM: [in another,](https://www.facebook.com/nemponthu/videos/1029269035832763) an AI teacher, bus driver, and doctor look desperately into the camera while the narrator lists how much less they would earn with the tax rates attributed to the Tisza.

[This “leaked tax increase plan” originates from an anonymous article published](https://telex.hu/belfold/2025/08/30/kampany-fidesz-tisza-adougy-magyar-peter-tarr-zoltan-kommunikacio) in Index, which is owned by Lőrinc Mészáros, and which discussed the Tisza Party’s alleged intention to increase taxes. Magyar almost immediately denied the content of the article, and Index has so far been unable to prove its authenticity, while the Fidesz media machine is already treating it as a fait accompli and is advertising on every possible platform how badly it would affect people. Viktor Orbán even announced in Kötcsén that [he would organize a national consultation](https://telex.hu/belfold/2025/09/07/orban-viktor-nemzeti-konzultacio-tisza-part-adoemelesi-tervek) in this regard.

# Two journalists fired from ATV for “unprofessional use of artificial intelligence”

September 30, 2025 – 07:51


updated

ATV also got rid of two of its online editors after the channel

[broadcast Viktor Orbán's speech on the first day of the autumn session of parliament in the morning](https://telex.hu/belfold/2025/09/22/atv-hu-orban-viktor-paralmenti-beszede-joslas-magyarorszagot-naggya-tenni), which the prime minister only delivered in the afternoon.

– the channel's communications officer confirmed the information from Telex.

As [we reported](https://telex.hu/belfold/2025/09/22/atv-hu-orban-viktor-paralmenti-beszede-joslas-magyarorszagot-naggya-tenni) , on September 22nd at 9:09 an article was published on atv.hu, which reviewed Viktor Orbán’s speech [on the first day](https://telex.hu/belfold/2025/09/22/parlament-oszi-ulesszak-elso-nap-orban-viktor-felszolalas-napirend-elott) of the autumn session of parliament – however, the prime minister only rose to speak at 1:00 p.m. that day, so ATV’s online platform essentially reported on a future event. The article was amended at 11:30 a.m. so that it now refers exclusively to Orbán’s post, and the elements of the “delivered” parliamentary speech were omitted.

After the incident became public, the channel wrote to Telex that the editorial staff had made a serious professional mistake, which would have consequences. ATV revealed the following about the matter on Wednesday in response to our inquiry (we are publishing the statement in full at the channel's request):


"Following ATV's internal investigation, two employees left the institution, but the events did not happen as reported in the press last night. One of the atv.hu journalists was held accountable for the unprofessional use of artificial intelligence, and the newspaper's editor-in-chief was held accountable for passive behavior, i.e., an offense of omission. Both admitted their mistakes and left the institution."

We also asked ATV how common it is that articles are written with AI, and the channel replied that "texts written with artificial intelligence are not accepted, which is also why the colleague left."

*Our article has been updated with additional response from ATV.*

RTPP2BUC.title: AI gebruiken voor artikelen: 'Belangrijk dat redacties transparant zijn' [AUTO-TRANSLATED IN ARC]
RTPP2BUC.markdown:
# Using AI for articles: 'Important that newsrooms are transparent'

- Thomas Michel - Online Editor 

When writer Thomas Heerma van Voss read a mention of his new book **Het Archief** on the website of the fashion magazine *Harper's Bazaar* , he was surprised by the text. How his book was described did not match the story at all.

Mentions of other books also turned out to be incorrect. "I had come across sloppy summaries before, but none of the text I read seemed to apply to my book," writes the author in a[column](https://www.de-lage-landen.com/article/kunstmatige-intelligentie/).

Heerma van Voss suspected that the text had been written by artificial intelligence and decided to email the editors. He requested that the editors take the article about the books offline and asked for a correction. He also expressed his suspicions regarding the use of artificial intelligence.

To put it to the test, the author himself asked the AI system ChatGPT what his book was about. This produced a text similar to the one the magazine published.

## Extremely reprehensible

In response to his email, the magazine informed him that the review had been modified into a text whose content was correct, but which lacked a written correction. The magazine also did not acknowledge that it used an AI tool.

The magazine has since provided a response to the NOS and acknowledged that "unfortunately, it turned out that artificial intelligence was indeed used to write the article." The piece has been taken offline.

The use of AI for writing articles is not in accordance with our internal guidelines and rules. We deeply regret the course of events and appropriate measures have been taken. We take our journalistic role seriously and will ensure that this does not happen again in the future.

## Erosion of the truth

Heerma van Voss calls the incident extremely reprehensible. According to him, newspapers and magazines must do their best "not to become a repository for the most idiotic and offensive disinformation." He considers it an example of "further erosion of the truth."

The incident raises the question of whether newsrooms are using AI more frequently to write articles.

Laurens Vreekamp is a journalist and wrote a book about artificial intelligence. He recognizes Thomas Heerma van Voss's story. According to him, the texts of AI-generated articles are usually grammatically and linguistically correct, but the content can be incorrect. "It is a language model, not a truth model."

Article writing by AI tools occurs primarily in the United States for "websites that derive their right to exist from the number of visitors. The more traffic a website generates, the more money it brings in from advertisers," says Vreekamp. "The content of the website is then merely a means to achieve that. And you can save on that content by having the site written by tools like ChatGPT."

## Disclaimer required

Many quality media outlets have established rules for the use of AI following the introduction of ChatGPT. "In virtually all the guidelines I have seen, editors are prohibited from having articles written by AI language tools." If this does happen, it is important that a disclaimer is included with the article stating that this has been done, Vreekamp states.

Hannes Cools, ** **media researcher and AI expert at the University of Amsterdam, confirms this. He knows of examples of misuse of artificial intelligence by newsrooms.

A Belgian newspaper published an obituary about someone that contained up to five errors, says Cools. "According to that article, someone supposedly had more children than they actually did." The newspaper subsequently received a phone call from the next of kin requesting a correction.

According to Cools, it is difficult for the reader to determine what was created by an AI tool. "The reader also does not know whether a text has been rewritten or reviewed by a final editor."

It is therefore good for an article to include a footnote if it was generated by an AI bot or language model, Cool believes. He notes, however, that research has shown readers trust an article less if it states that it was created by artificial intelligence.

## Transparency

"When you look at regulations, transparency is central," says the researcher. "Media organizations do not fall under the European Union's AI Act, but they do follow these rules," Cools explains. According to Vreekamp, in practice this means that quality media often do not use AI.

"I do see that AI is being used to check texts for grammar, ** **but that there is no disclaimer in these kinds of cases. That needs to change," says researcher Cools. "It is not always opportune to disclose which tools were used, but it is necessary."

"If newsrooms fail to explain why something was created using artificial intelligence and this is discovered, they lose face, and that harms the organization." It is therefore important that they consistently explain when and why AI is used, concludes the researcher.

## Make NOS your preferred source on Google

With a new Google feature, you can now decide for yourself which sources you see first when you search. This way, you will never miss the latest news from the NOS again.

9MMHAGPX.title: Børsen siger farvel til alle korrekturlæsere – erstatter dem med AI [AUTO-TRANSLATED IN ARC]
9MMHAGPX.markdown:
A handful of hourly-paid proofreaders, who have so far ensured that Dagbladet Børsen is published without spelling or grammatical errors, will no longer be part of the newspaper's team.

This is the consequence of the fact that the management at Børsen has decided to close down the proofreading department and replace the live proofreaders with an AI-based solution.

This is what editor-in-chief Nikolaj Sommer tells Journalisten.

"We have been happy with our proofreaders, who have done a good job. But this is one of the areas where technological developments have really made a difference. And we therefore assess that we can get an AI-based solution that will be able to do a similar job," he explains.

## Concerned about quality

The editor-in-chief explains that Børsen has already tested the new system, which according to him delivers at a high level.

"These large LLM models (large language models, ed.) can now not only correct words, but also understand words in context at such a high level that we feel comfortable with it," says Nikolaj Sommer.

**Michael Solgaard**, shop steward

However, management's assurances do not reassure all employees that quality will not be compromised when the live proofreaders are replaced with artificial intelligence, says union representative for the DJ members at Børsen, Michael Solgaard.

"Of course I listen when they say that it can be done without these employees. But having said that, I am of course also concerned about what this means for the quality of our product. Because of course proofreading is an important part of quality," he says.

At the same time, the shop steward adds that he is of course in favor of Børsen using the money in the most optimal way.

“I have to trust that our management will make sensible and correct decisions,” says Michael Solgaard.

## Hoping for more employees

Editor-in-chief Nikolaj Sommer emphasizes that the closure of the proofreading department is not a cost-cutting exercise. In fact, the hope is that the introduction of AI may eventually lead to more employees.

"The only way we can ensure that there are still jobs at Børsen is by seizing the technological opportunities that exist. It is an obligation for management. Otherwise, we will end up in a place where our competitors can do it faster and better," says Nikolaj Sommer.

“But if we do it right, I only believe that over time it can lead to us having more employees at Børsen, not fewer,” says Nikolaj Sommer.

**Nikolaj Sommer**, editor-in-chief

Some of the proofreaders that Børsen is now waving goodbye to have been at the newspaper for several years, and the editor-in-chief therefore understands well that the news, which was announced on Thursday, will hit home among the newspaper's employees.

"I understand that it can be a difficult story for an employee to take in. In that way, it's not nice news. But that's how it has to be. Where it makes sense - and it really does here - we have to seize the technological opportunities," says Nikolaj Sommer.

## 3 Comments

Regards Niels R. Laugesen, editorial secretary, language expert etc. at Børsen for 40 years.

what is currently in the newspaper and can inform and debate.

AI only disseminates data on request, when someone searches.

Proofreaders can be more outreaching and offensive in sharing knowledge. AI cannot be personified.

# Regulator demands "letter of principles" from CNN regarding the use of artificial intelligence.

This is the first time the ERC (Regulatory Entity for the Media) has commented on AI-generated content in a television news program. The issue concerned the segment "Pulsómetro," related to the legislative election debates.

The Regulatory Authority for Social Communication (ERC) wants CNN Portugal to publish a charter of principles for the use of artificial intelligence (AI), after the channel **used this technology in a segment about electoral debates** as part of the campaign for the 2024 legislative elections.

## Choose ECO as your preferred font on Google.

[To choose](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=https%3A%2F%2Feco.sapo.pt%2F)

**In a statement, the ERC (Regulatory Entity for the Media) says that CNN Portugal** needs to " **prepare and publish a charter of principles on the use of artificial intelligence in its newsroom** , should it continue producing news content using AI tools."

This measure aims to " **guarantee the integrity of both the content resulting from this technology and the prerogatives inherent to journalistic activity** , and to make transparent to viewers the type of tasks performed by these systems – editorial and/or non-editorial".

**This is the first time the ERC (Regulatory Entity for the Media) has commented on AI-generated content within a television news program** . According to the regulator, media outlets that use AI "must follow codes of good practice and make it explicit to the public whether these systems are used only as adjuncts to tasks or whether they replace journalistic work in the production of content."

**The issue concerned the segment "Pulsómetro** ," part of CNN's "Decisão 24" program, which prompted a complaint forwarded by the National Elections Commission regarding the regulator.

Developed in partnership with Augusta Labs, the "Pulsometer" was launched by CNN Portugal during the election campaign for the 2024 legislative elections. **The tool was a "social media sentiment indicator" that ****analyzed "millions of data points on social media in real time** , on pages considered neutral," in order to "take the temperature" of each of the electoral debates, [CNN](https://cnnportugal.iol.pt/pulsometro/cnn-portugal/cnn-portugal-lanca-pulsometro-para-os-debates-eleitorais/20240205/65c14035d34e371fc0bcc1d0) explained at the time of its launch.

According to the channel, "only opinions relating to the comparative performance of the candidates present in each debate were considered, interpreted through an LLM (' *large language model* ', a natural language model) capable of performing sentiment analysis on the various interactions identified."

In its assessment of the case, the ERC also recalls the **ten general principles contained in the Paris Charter on Journalism and AI** . This document, launched by the international organization Reporters Without Borders (RSF) in conjunction with 16 partners, aims to define ethical principles and standards for journalists, newsrooms, and media outlets in their relationship with artificial intelligence.
